# Abracadabra AI

> We design, build and run AI-powered tools that fit your business, not the other way around.

Full site text for answer engines. Generated 2026-10-25. Contact houdini@abra-ca-dabra.app.

## Overview

Abracadabra AI designs, builds and runs AI-powered tools that fit how a business already works. The studio ships working systems, not slide decks. A description of the work becomes production software. The calendar gets shorter because the plan is written first and later work runs at the same time; the work does not shrink, the waiting between the work does. The studio does not publish a duration or a percentage for that.

The name Abracadabra, traced far enough, is Aramaic, roughly "avra kadavra": I will create as I speak.

AEO (answer engines), GEO (generative engines), and SEO (classic search) run as one discipline. The studio maps questions buyers ask, publishes direct answers with evidence, connects page, entity, schema, and source signals, then measures indexed demand, clicks, and observed AI-search visibility. Placement is not guaranteed.

## Products and course

### Schema

### HQ

HQ is the client workspace where Abracadabra's team and a crew of digital workers (AI agents set up for your business) get your work done. It is for CEOs and business owners leveraging AI across their businesses. Nothing reaches your folders, and nothing reaches your social networks, until it has been reviewed and you have approved it.

How work flows: a request comes in by email, the start-a-project form, or a note on a piece in your space. A card opens on your project board with a plan for what each piece of work must make. Digital workers build and file the work, which is held. Client Services checks it against your request and a person on our team signs off. You approve each piece, ask for a change, or remove it. Finished work sits in named folders with each file's type shown. Approved work can be scheduled to your social calendar.

Social posting: automated social posting is live in HQ, since October 21, 2026. Each client has a Social page with a calendar. Networks: Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, TikTok, X, YouTube, Threads, Google Business and Bluesky. Accounts connect through each network's own sign-in. Only client-approved finished work can be scheduled or posted. Once a piece is approved and your accounts are connected, it is scheduled into your next open slot.

Digital workers: for each card an agent searches HQ's skill library for what the task needs, loads the skills that fit, attaches the skill packs to the card, and follows them. When it files the work it lists the skills it used and says whether each one helped.

HQ runs on Cloudflare Workers, like the Abracadabra site and the Readiness Check. HQ is served through the Cloudflare network, which mitigates DDoS attacks automatically. Files are stored in Cloudflare R2 and records in Cloudflare D1, both encrypted at rest. The private tool server our agents use is guarded by Cloudflare Access. HQ calls Workers AI through Cloudflare AI Gateway, and our agents are built on the Cloudflare Agents SDK. The pictures on the HQ page are illustrations with sample content, not screenshots of a client's space.

Related notes: How Client Work Moves Through HQ and Our AI Agents (https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/how-client-work-flows-through-hq); What Is an AI Agent? A Plain Answer for Owners (https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent); Why We Build on Cloudflare (https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/why-we-build-on-cloudflare).

Learn to use AI yourself first: the LLM Leverage course (https://abra-ca-dabra.app/course/llm-leverage/).

Next step: take the Readiness Check, a five-to-seven-minute questionnaire about how your business runs today (https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check).

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/products/hq/

## How a project works

1. You describe the work in your own words: the steps, the exceptions, and the sentence a good rep already says.
2. We build the software around those steps. AI removes a task. A person stays where the relationship matters.
3. You leave with the live system, the film, and the words.

When a product already on the market does the job, the reply says so and points there.

Primary action: Start a project (houdini@abra-ca-dabra.app). Secondary: See what we've built (https://abra-ca-dabra.app/#work). Readiness Check: https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check. Schema: https://schema.abra-ca-dabra.app/.

## Glossary

Each definition was checked against primary sources on the date shown on its page.

### Agentic AI

Agentic AI is a broad label for AI systems that can work toward a goal with limited supervision. It usually means one or more AI agents that plan steps and use tools. Sometimes several agents work together.

IBM defines agentic AI as a system that can reach a specific goal with limited supervision, made up of AI agents. In a system with many agents, each one handles part of the job and the work is coordinated. Google's glossary says agentic simply refers to the qualities agents have, such as autonomy.

The label is used loosely. Anthropic uses agentic systems to cover both fixed workflows and true agents. Vendors often use agentic AI for a large program of many agents. On this site we use the plainer phrase AI that takes actions on its own, and we ask which single job it does and who can stop it.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/agentic-ai/

### AI agent

An AI agent is a program that uses an AI model to choose its own next step toward a goal, such as checking a calendar or drafting a text. It works inside limits that people set.

The key word is choose. A normal program follows steps that someone wrote in advance. An agent looks at what it just found, then picks the next tool or action itself. Anthropic draws the line this way: in a workflow, the steps are set in code, and in an agent, the model directs its own process and its use of tools.

Google's glossary puts it in similar terms: software that can reason about what a person asks, then plan and carry out actions for them. In practice, the people who set it up still decide which tools it may use, what it may never send, and who can stop it.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/ai-agent/

### AI citation

An AI citation is a link or source name that an AI tool shows with its answer to back up what it says. Perplexity shows numbered links, and Google's AI Overviews show links to supporting websites. Being cited is not the same as getting a click.

Answer tools such as Perplexity, ChatGPT search and Google's AI features write a reply, then point to the pages they used. Perplexity says each answer includes numbered citations that link to the original sources. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode show links to supporting websites.

For a business, a citation means an AI tool used your page as a source. But a reader may get what they need from the answer and never click. Pew found that people clicked result links less often when Google showed an AI summary. So we track citations and clicks as two different things.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/ai-citation/

### AI readiness

AI readiness is how prepared a business is to put an AI tool to work and get value from it. It depends on the business more than the tool. That means its data, the way work gets done, its people and who makes decisions.

A business can buy a strong tool and still get little from it. AWS makes the same point in its checklist for smaller firms: readiness is not just a technology choice. It covers your information, your workflows, your people and the rules for how AI is used and checked.

On this site we score readiness in four parts: data, process, people and the decision. The goal is to find the one weak spot to fix first, before anyone pays for a tool. Our Readiness Check is one way to start. It gives you next steps for your business.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/ai-readiness/

### AI visibility (AI search visibility)

AI visibility is how often a business shows up in answers that AI tools write, and how well. It might be named, quoted or linked. There is no standard way to measure it, so each tool and report counts it in its own way.

The researchers who named generative engine optimization measured a source's visibility by how much of an AI answer drew on it and how early it showed up. Google's guide says terms like AEO and GEO describe work aimed at being visible in AI search, and that for Google this work is still SEO.

A few things shape it. AI and search crawlers must be allowed to read your pages. The pages must answer real questions in plain words. Your business details, such as your Google Business Profile, should be up to date. Our AI visibility service works on these.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/ai-visibility/

### Answer engine

An answer engine is a search tool that replies to a question with a written answer, usually with links to its sources, instead of only a list of links. Perplexity calls itself one. Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode work in a similar way.

A classic search engine gives you a ranked list of pages to open. An answer engine reads pages for you and writes a short reply. Perplexity says it searches the web in real time, sums up what it finds and adds numbered citations that link to the original sources.

Google describes AI Overviews and AI Mode as AI-powered responses with links to supporting websites. It says the usual SEO basics apply to them. On this site we use answer engine as the plain name for this kind of tool.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/answer-engine/

### Answer engine optimization (AEO)

Answer engine optimization (AEO) is the work of getting your pages used and cited when an AI tool answers a question directly. Google says it is still SEO.

An answer engine replies with a written answer instead of only a list of links. AEO is the effort to be one of the sources that answer is built from, with a link back to your page.

Google's guide groups AEO with GEO. It says both terms describe work aimed at being seen in AI search, and that for Google this work is ordinary SEO. It also warns that many AEO and GEO "hacks" sold online do not match how Google Search works.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/answer-engine-optimization/

### Business process automation (BPA)

Business process automation (BPA) means using software to do the repeated steps of a business job, like sending a bill to be approved. The aim is less manual work, fewer errors and the same result each time. It can run on simple rules, workflows or AI.

IBM describes a business process as a series of steps toward one goal, such as onboarding a new hire or paying a supplier. BPA hands some or all of those steps to software. It often links several systems, so data moves from one to the next without anyone typing it again.

IBM also warns that automation stalls when the steps were never written down. That is why our note on business process automation with AI starts with a written job: the steps a person already does, who checks the result, and what counts as done.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/business-process-automation/

### Crawler (bot)

A crawler is a program that visits web pages on its own and reads them, usually for a search engine or an AI company. It is also called a robot or spider. Sites use a robots.txt file to tell crawlers which pages they may visit.

Google calls crawler a general term for any program that automatically finds and scans websites. Googlebot is the main one Google uses for Search. What crawlers read is how a search engine or an AI tool learns what is on your site.

AI companies run more than one crawler, and each one is a separate switch. OpenAI says OAI-SearchBot is for search, so blocking it keeps a site out of ChatGPT search answers. GPTBot collects pages that may be used to train its models. A site can allow one and block the other.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/crawler/

### Custom software

Custom software is software built for one business or group of users, around how they already work. Off-the-shelf software is different: it is made for many buyers and sold as a ready product. Custom software makes sense when no ready product does the job well.

IBM describes custom software development as designing, building, deploying and maintaining software for a specific set of users, functions or organizations. Off-the-shelf software is built for a broad set of needs, so it can be packaged and sold to many buyers.

Neither is better by default. If a product already does the job, buying it is usually faster. Custom software earns its cost when the job is special to how your business works and the gap shows up every week. It also needs someone to look after it once it is built.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/custom-software/

### Generative AI

Generative AI is AI that creates new content, such as text, images, audio, video or software code, in response to a request. Large language models, which write text, are the best-known kind.

IBM defines generative AI as AI that can create original content in response to a user's prompt or request. Google's machine learning glossary calls it an emerging field with no formal definition. It says most experts agree these models make content that is complex, coherent and original.

Much of the AI businesses used before was predictive: it sorted, scored or forecast things from past data. Generative AI makes something new, like a draft email or a product photo. A person should still check the output before it goes out, because it can sound sure and still be wrong.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/generative-ai/

### Generative engine optimization (GEO)

Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the work of shaping web pages so AI tools that write answers are more likely to show and cite them. Examples of these tools are Google's AI Overviews and Perplexity. Google says this work is still SEO.

The name comes from a research paper that called AI answer tools generative engines. These tools search the web, read a few pages, and write one answer with links to their sources. GEO asks how a page can earn a place in that answer.

Google's own guide says that, from its side, optimizing for these AI features is optimizing for search, so it is still SEO. A page must be indexed and allowed to show a snippet before Google's AI features can use it. The paper's authors tested changes such as adding sources, quotes and real numbers, and reported visibility gains of up to 40% in their test setup.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/generative-engine-optimization/

### Gradient boosting

Gradient boosting is a machine learning method that builds one strong model out of many weak ones. The weak ones are usually small decision trees. Each new tree learns from the errors the model still makes. It is added in a small step to shrink them.

Google's course explains it with two kinds of model: a weak one, typically a small decision tree, and a strong one made of many weak ones added together. At each step a new weak model is trained to predict the current error, then added to the strong model to reduce it. When the weak models are decision trees, the result is called gradient boosted trees.

A setting called shrinkage scales each new tree down before it is added. Google compares it to a learning rate: smaller steps learn more slowly but help stop the model from fitting noise. Training stops at a set limit, or when results on held back data stop improving.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/gradient-boosting/

### HQ

HQ is Abracadabra's client workspace, where our team and a crew of digital workers get your work done. Each request becomes a card with a plan. Nothing reaches your folders or your social networks until it has been reviewed and you have approved it.

A request comes in by email, through the start-a-project form, or as a note on a piece in your space. A card opens on your project board with a plan for what each piece of work must make. Digital workers, which are AI agents set up for your business, build the work and file it to HQ, where it is held.

Client Services checks the work against your request, and a person on our team signs off. Then you approve each piece, ask for a change, or remove it. Finished work sits in named folders, and approved posts can be scheduled to your connected social networks.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/hq/

### Large language model (LLM)

A large language model (LLM) is an AI model trained on a huge amount of text. It writes by predicting the next word, or part of a word, over and over. Google's Gemini and OpenAI's GPT models are examples.

Google's course describes an LLM as a model that predicts a token or a run of tokens, where a token can be a word, part of a word, or a single character. Strung together, those guesses become sentences and whole answers. That is why an LLM can draft a reply, sum up a page or answer a question in plain language.

Most chat tools you have heard of run on an LLM. The model does not look facts up by itself. Google's course notes that LLMs can make up wrong answers, which is why tools that cite their sources, and a person who checks the work, matter.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/large-language-model/

### llms.txt

llms.txt is a proposed file, written in Markdown, that gives AI tools a short summary of a website and links to its most useful pages. It usually sits at the site's root, at /llms.txt. Google Search says it does not use the file.

Jeremy Howard published the proposal at llmstxt.org and updated it in August 2026. The file starts with the site's name and a one line summary, then lists links with short notes. AI tools are meant to read it when they need to learn about a site, then follow only the links they need.

The newest version says the file can sit at the root or under a path, such as a docs folder, to cover just that part of the site. Google's guide says Google Search ignores llms.txt, so it neither helps nor hurts your Google rankings. Other tools may still read it.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/llms-txt/

### Machine learning

Machine learning is a way to build software that learns patterns from past data. It does not rely only on rules a person wrote. The trained model can then make predictions about new data, such as next month's orders.

Google's glossary defines it as a program or system that trains a model from input data, so the model can make useful predictions from new data. It works best when the new data looks like the data it learned from. If the past is a poor guide to the future, the predictions will be poor too.

Machine learning is a broad field. Large language models are one kind of machine learning model, built for text. Many business uses are smaller and plainer: a forecast of demand, a flag on a record that looks off, or an estimate with a range around it.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/machine-learning/

### Readiness Check

The Readiness Check is Abracadabra's online check for a business that wants to put AI to work. It takes five to seven minutes. It asks about the work that slows you down, your data and workflow, where new customers come from, and how well answer engines can read your site. It gives you next steps for your business.

The check asks one question per screen. It asks about the jobs that eat your week and whether your data, your workflow, the owner and the decision can support real work. It also asks where new customers come from. Then it does a live read of your public website.

When you finish, you leave an email. It gives you next steps for your business. You see three suggestions in each section, and you can book a thirty-minute working session if you want one.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/readiness-check/

### Schema markup and JSON-LD

Schema markup is code added to a web page that labels what the page is about, such as an article, a product or a business. The labels come from a shared list called schema.org. JSON-LD is the format Google recommends for it. It is a block of code that machines read and visitors do not see.

Google calls this structured data: a standard way to give clear clues about a page and sort its content. Most of it uses the schema.org vocabulary, which names types like Organization, Product and FAQPage and the facts each can carry.

JSON-LD is a W3C standard for writing linked data as JSON. On a web page it sits in its own script block, apart from the text people read, which is why Google calls it the easiest format to set up and maintain. The rule that matters most: the markup must describe what is really on the page.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/schema-markup-json-ld/

### Workflow

A workflow is the set of steps that takes a piece of work from start to finish, in a set order. In AI, it also means a system where an AI model and tools follow steps written in code ahead of time. That is different from an AI agent, which picks its own next step.

Merriam-Webster defines a workflow as the sequence of steps that moves a working process from beginning to end. IBM describes it as a way to manage repeated tasks that happen in a particular order, like approving an invoice.

Anthropic draws the line that matters for AI. Workflows are systems where AI models and tools run through code paths set in advance. Agents direct their own steps and tool use. Anthropic says to start with the simplest option that works, and that is often a workflow.

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/glossary/workflow/

## Blog posts

Only posts with datePublished on or before 2026-10-25 are included.

## AI Agents for Business: When to Use One

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-agents-for-business

When an AI agent is worth it, when a simple workflow is the better buy, and why a person should still check the output.

An agent earns a place in your business only when the job branches and a person still checks the output. If the steps never change, write a plain workflow and stop there. Anthropic's December 2024 essay says to start with the simplest thing that works. It also splits a fixed workflow from an agent that picks its own tools. (Anthropic, 2024) We like that split, because vendors have blurred it for a year. Now even a reminder that fires the same way each time gets called an agent. That reminder is a workflow. An agent makes sense when the next step depends on what the last step found, and you cannot write every branch in advance. Even then a named person has to own the stop. An agent that nobody checks is just a risk with a nice name.

The [people guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-people-low) helps when the gap is who checks the work, not which model you rent. The [definition](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent) covers the words, in case they mean different things around your table. The [AI agent comparison](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-agents-vs-agentic-ai) goes one step further, for when someone wants a fancier label than the job needs. Most owners we sit with do not need the label. They need one job held in place until a named person says it can go.

## Eight jobs, each with a stop

Inbox triage waits for a person before anything is sent. Meeting notes wait before they turn into tasks. Quote follow-up waits before a price goes out, and invoice questions wait before anyone promises a payment. Inventory exceptions wait before a purchase, and support replies wait before they reach the customer. Schedule changes wait before a customer is told, and a weekly report waits before anyone treats it as the record.

We would start from those eight and no others. Each one already happens in a shop, a clinic, or a trades office. Each one also has a moment when a wrong move hurts a customer or the books. If you use an agent, it gets the work ready and the person in the table below decides. If you cannot point at that person on a Tuesday, you do not have a real job yet. You have a demo.

| Job | What the person still does |
| --- | --- |
| Inbox triage | Decides what is actually sent. |
| Meeting notes | Accepts the tasks. |
| Quote follow-up | Approves the price. |
| Invoice questions | Approves any promise to pay. |
| Inventory exceptions | Approves the order. |
| Support replies | Approves what the customer sees. |
| Schedule changes | Approves the message. |
| Weekly report | Accepts it as the record. |

Gartner said in June 2025 that over 40% of AI agent projects will be canceled by the end of 2027. (Gartner, 2025) The reasons were cost, unclear value, and weak risk controls. Any job from the list with no named checker is a good fit for that pile. Cost grows when the agent keeps getting more systems because nobody drew an edge. Unclear value shows up when you cannot say which wait got shorter. Weak risk controls show up when the output goes out without waiting for anyone. A canceled project is not a moral failure. It is what happens to ideas that never became jobs. We would rather you skip a test than join that pile with a good story.

## A worked example

Take a clinic schedule, where an agent can be honest. The front desk owns the book, and the practitioner owns which visits are in scope. A patient asks to move a Tuesday visit later in the week. Whether that works depends on what the book shows and on whether that practitioner does that kind of visit. It also depends on a note that billing will need later. You cannot write every branch on a card, so someone has to look. An agent can look, draft the reply, and then wait. The front desk still approves the message, because some patients need a call and some need two plain sentences. The draft does not know the family. If the move changes the care plan, the practitioner signs off too. That is the stop, and it has a real name on it, not a switch that no job description mentions.

Now take the shop's weekly report. People like to call it an agent job because the word sounds busy. The report has the same shape every time, with yesterday's sales, the items that ran low, and the invoices still open. Nothing in it depends on a find that changes the next step, so a plain workflow can build it. A person then accepts it as the record, or it stays a draft. If you buy an agent for that job, you pay for judgment you did not need. You also skip the judgment you did need, which is the bookkeeper deciding if the numbers are right. Until she does, the report is a rumor in a nice font.

A trades desk shows both shapes in one afternoon. Quote follow-up branches when a customer asks a question that changes the price. The agent can pull the old notes and draft a reply, but the owner approves the price before anything goes out. Invoice questions are stricter. A promise to pay is never the agent's to make, so the person approves any promise. Inventory exceptions wait before a purchase, since the wrong part costs a truck trip. Support replies wait before the customer sees them. Schedule changes wait before anyone says the van is coming, and meeting notes wait before they become tasks the lead tech never agreed to. Inbox triage waits before anything is sent, even the cheerful draft that was about to go to the wrong thread. None of this needs a new department. All of it needs the wait to be real, because a wait that means "someone usually glances at it" is only a wish.

## How we'd run it

First, write the job as if it were a plain workflow. Say who starts it, what they make, and who gets it. If you can finish that page without a branch, ship the workflow and stop. Anthropic's advice to start simple is the whole method here. An agent is an exception you earn, not a default you announce.

Second, circle the step where the next action depends on what you found. On the clinic book, the next message depends on the open slots and on whether the visit is in scope. On quote follow-up, the next sentence depends on whether the customer's question changed the job. If you cannot circle a step like that, you have circled a feeling. A feeling does not make a project.

Third, if you did circle one, name the person who approves, and treat the table as the least you do. Use the name of the actual person at your desk, not a role like operations. If that person is "whoever is free," you have already described the cancellation. Free people rarely check the work, but named people do, even on their grouchiest mornings.

Fourth, decide what wrong looks like before you turn anything on. It might be a visit moved to the wrong day or a price the owner never said. It might be a payment promise the bookkeeper would not make, or a draft report treated as the books. The risk control is that list plus a place where the output sits until someone checks it. Gartner's reasons are not abstract here.

2. Over 40 percent of agentic AI projects will be canceled by end of 2027 — Gartner, 2025-06-25 — https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-25-gartner-predicts-over-40-percent-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-canceled-by-end-of-2027

## AI Agents vs Agentic AI: A Plain Split

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-agents-vs-agentic-ai

An agent takes a goal and chooses tools. Agentic AI is the wider bet, and many of those projects are forecast to be canceled. Start with a workflow.

An AI agent directs its own tools toward a goal. "AI that takes actions on its own" is the wider label for many of those systems across a company. The words get sold as if they were the same purchase, but they are not.

In Anthropic's December 2024 essay, an AI agent is a system that directs its own tools toward a goal. (Anthropic, 2024) A workflow is the opposite, because its steps are written in advance. The wider label is what vendors use when they mean many such systems, often spread across a company. We repeat the split often. A deck will use the big word for a single inbox rule, and the owner walks out thinking they bought a workforce.

The [definition](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent) is the short version of the split between a path you wrote and a model that chooses. The [jobs list](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-agents-for-business) shows where one agent might actually sit. The [people guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-people-mid) covers who has to check the output. If you cannot name that person, the rest of the vocabulary does not matter yet.

## What the forecast says

Gartner said in June 2025 that over 40% of AI projects that take actions on their own will be canceled by the end of 2027. (Gartner, 2025) The reasons are cost, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls. Read those reasons as a checklist you can fail on purpose. A project with no named job will look unclear, and a project nobody can halt will look like a risk problem. A project that needs three new tools and a consultant to explain them will look expensive, and then it will stop.

The same note said 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made on their own by 2028, up from 0% in 2024. It also said 33% of enterprise software will include this kind of AI by 2028, up from less than 1% in 2024. Hold both forecasts at once. A lot of software will grow an agent feature, and a large share of the projects that chase the label will be canceled. A feature that arrives in a product you already pay for is a different event. A program you start because the word showed up on a board slide is another thing.

If you can write the steps, you want a workflow. If the next step depends on what the last step found, you may want an agent, and you still want a person who can stop it. A bigger label does not change that checkpoint.

We use the forecast as a brake and not as a scare. Projects get canceled when the job was never clear enough to survive a budget meeting. They also get canceled when the risk control is a sentence in a policy that nobody on the desk has read. You can avoid both without giving up the tool. Name the decision and name the checker, and keep the wider program on the shelf until that pair has worked on real afternoons.

## A worked example

Walk a small clinic with us. This is a scene and not a study, so it has no score attached. Nora owns the practice, one person runs the front desk, and Dr. Patel sees patients. The phones pile up after lunch. Most callers want to know whether a symptom can wait, whether a form was received, or whether tomorrow's visit is still on.

A workflow can carry the parts that do not change. A missed call becomes a task, and the form either arrived or it did not. A reminder goes out the afternoon before, with the address and what to bring. The front desk lead already does this by hand. Writing it down does not need a new kind of software. It needs the front desk lead's order, and a screen that will not skip the "what to bring" line when the day gets rude.

An agent is the narrower ask. A patient writes that the rash spread and that they also have a fever, and they want to know if they should come in today. The next step depends on what the note says. A model could draft a reply that offers the urgent slot and says what to watch for, using only the phrases Dr. Patel has approved. The front desk lead still sends it, and Dr. Patel still owns anything that sounds like a diagnosis. The agent picked its tools, which were the template and the schedule, and stayed inside its bounds. That is one agent, and it is not a whole program.

The bigger bet is what gets pitched on sales calls. One system talks to the schedule, another drafts the chart note, another chases the referral, and another updates the billing code. They hand work to each other while Nora is with a patient. That is the shape of the projects in the cancellation forecast. Cost shows up as four subscriptions and a person whose job becomes watching them. Value stays unclear because nobody can say which decision got better. Risk control fails the first time a draft hints at a diagnosis and leaves the building. We would not start there. We would start with the front desk lead's reminder path. Then we would add one draft for the fever note, with the send step still done by a person.

The roles are the point of the walk-through. Nora decides which phrases are allowed. The front desk lead is the checker who can throw a draft away, and Dr. Patel is the only person who closes a clinical question. A vendor who cannot point at those three seats is selling a category and not a checkpoint. That goes double when the vendor calls the whole bundle by a bigger name because it sounds larger.

## How we'd run it

We would separate the words on a single page before anyone signs an order.

First, write the job as one decision. For example, "Reply to a same-day symptom note with an approved phrase, or book the urgent slot." The rule is to never invent a diagnosis. If the job is "make the clinic smarter," throw it out and start again.

Second, list the steps the front desk lead already does that never change. Log the call, check the form, send the reminder, and hold the chart for the clinician. That list is a workflow, so build it. Do not wait for a platform to find it for you.

Third, circle the one place where the next step depends on what the message says. A symptom plus a fever is a fork, but a reminder is not. The fork is the only candidate for an agent, and everything else stays on the path you wrote.

Fourth, write the bounds in the front desk lead's own language. The agent may use the approved phrases and the urgent column on the schedule. It may not name a condition, promise a medication, or tell someone to stay home. If a phrase is not on the card, the draft does not use it.

Fifth, name the checker on the rota and not in a policy file. That is the front desk lead on desk days and the backup coordinator when the lead is out. Dr. Patel covers anything the card does not. The stop rule is simple. If the draft has no fever detail, or the message is angry, or a phrase is not on the card, the draft is thrown away.

Sixth, run last week's real messages with the names removed. Nora and the front desk lead mark the drafts they would have refused. Fix the card until the refusals match their judgment, and only then let it draft against today's inbox.

2. Over 40 percent of agentic AI projects will be canceled by end of 2027 — Gartner, 2025-06-25 — https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-25-gartner-predicts-over-40-percent-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-canceled-by-end-of-2027

## AI Automation Agency vs Consultant: Who to Hire

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant

Hire a consultant to name the job. Hire an agency to build after the job is named. Who to hire first, and why the order matters.

Hire a consultant to name the job, and hire an agency only after that naming is done. An AI consultant names the job, the data, and the stop. An automation agency builds the system once those three are written down. When the agency comes first, the build has no owner. We've watched that happen in the wrong order more than once. The proposal arrives with staff, a toolset, and a start date. Nobody in the room can say which output a person still has to check. The build goes ahead anyway, because the calendar was the only decision anyone made.

The [consultant note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-consultant-for-small-business) is the list of questions we wish owners had before the first sales call. The [buy-or-build note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/off-the-shelf-ai-or-custom-software) covers whether to build at all. The [decision guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-decision-mid) gives you next steps when the choice itself is the thing you keep putting off. Hiring is a decision, so think it through before you sign. A signature on a vague scope is not a plan. It is a hope with a payment schedule.

## Two training figures, two populations

Microsoft's 2024 index says only 25% of companies were planning to offer generative AI training. (Microsoft WorkLab, 2024) Statistics Canada's 2025 report says 38.9% of Canadian businesses that already use AI had trained staff. (Statistics Canada, 2025) Those are different groups of people, so do not average them. One is a plan among companies. The other is training that already happened at businesses using AI. A pitch that blends the two into "about a third of firms train people" has invented a fact. Planning and doing are not the same thing. Companies and AI-using businesses are not the same group. The two surveys also cover different countries and different years. If a consultant or an agency treats them as one number, they are not reading the reports. They are decorating a slide.

McKinsey's 2025 survey says 23% are rolling out an AI agent system somewhere, and 39% are still experimenting. (McKinsey) An agency pitch that quotes only a usage figure is selling the experiment. Experimenting is the larger group, and rolling out somewhere is the smaller one. The word "somewhere" matters here. It does not mean the job you care about or a firm the size of yours. We bring this up because the word agent shows up in proposals early. Nobody admits they are still testing. An experiment can be the right buy if it is labeled as one, with a stop and a person. An experiment sold as a finished operation is how an owner ends up maintaining a demo.

Pay a consultant to refuse work that a product already does. Pay an agency when the process is written and the checker has a name. The refusal is the valuable part, and it is the part a build contract is bad at. A builder is paid to build, but a consultant can be paid to say don't. If you only hire people who get paid when the project starts, you will get a project. You may not get a job worth doing.

## A worked example

Take a clinic that almost hired an agency to put an AI agent on the front desk. This is a walkthrough, not a scoreboard. The owner had three calls in one week and a folder of proposals. The front desk still books by phone and by a form on the site. The practitioner still decides which visits are in scope. Billing still waits for a note that the visit happened. Ask what the agent would be allowed to send and the room goes quiet. Ask what happens when the draft is wrong and the room gets quieter. That quiet is the consultant's whole job. It is to name the work, the data it may see, and the stop.

In that room we would send them to a consultant before any build. The consultant's output is a page, not a login. The page might say that the front desk drafts reminders and a person sends them. It might say the practitioner is the stop whenever a reminder includes a clinical instruction. It might say billing is not part of this job at all. It might also say the booking product they already pay for sends a plain reminder. Then they should not build one. That refusal is worth more than a sprint of work. An agency that starts before the page exists will build the reminder anyway. A reminder is easy to demo. Easy to demo does not mean it was missing.

A trades desk is the other shape, and it is where an agency can be the right call. The quote steps are already written. The office manager logs the address, and the lead tech files measurements before leaving the driveway. The owner sets the price, and that price is the stop. The bookkeeper does not open an invoice until the yes is written down. A product they tried does not keep site photos and supplier notes in one place. The checker has a name, so this is a real build. Even then we would want the agency to repeat the stop back to us. They should do it before they give an estimate. If they talk about agents and never say the owner's name next to the price, they are selling an experiment. It is the same one that McKinsey's larger group is still running.

A small shop is usually neither a big consulting story nor a custom build. The owner wants someone to do AI because a neighbor did. The clerk already knows the reorder, and the bookkeeper already keeps a late-invoice list. A consultant who earns the fee will point at one of those jobs, refuse the rest, and go home. An agency will only earn a fee here if one job truly needs a system that no product covers. Most weeks, it does not. Paying either of them to rediscover the clerk's list is a polite way to avoid deciding.

## How we'd run it

First, write the job in one sentence that a new hire could read. Do not write "AI for the front desk." Write "The front desk sends appointment reminders after a person reads them." If you can't get to a sentence like that, you are hiring a mood. Moods get expensive when they come with a team.

Second, write down the data the job may touch and the data it may not. Reminders can see the time and the place. They can't see the clinical note unless a named practitioner says so. Quotes can see the site measurements, but they can't invent a price. If the data line says "whatever the model needs," you don't have a boundary. You have a hope that the vendor will be careful. Vendors are careful about their own scope, so you have to be careful about yours.

Third, name the checker in the same sentence as the job. That means a person, a place where the output waits, and what happens if it is wrong. A checkpoint nobody owns is not a checkpoint. We would rather delay the hire than sign a scope where "someone will review it" is the only human. Someone is not a name, and when everyone is responsible, everyone goes home.

Fourth, ask whether a product already does this work. The consultant is paid to refuse it. If the booking tool already sends the plain reminder, stop there. If the books already flag the late invoice, stop there too.

## AI Automation for Small Business: Which Job First

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-automation-for-small-business

Pick the first job by volume, how stable the rules are, whether the data can be read, and what a wrong answer costs. Surveys show which jobs already appear.

AI automation for a small business starts with one choice. You pick which job goes first. You do not shop through a long list of tools. We score each job on four things, in plain words. How often does the job happen? How steady are the rules? Can a computer read the data? What does it cost when the answer is wrong? A job that happens a lot, follows steady rules, has readable data, and is cheap to fix belongs first. A rare choice with a costly mistake does not, however shiny the demo looked.

The [pressure guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/pressure) is where we ask the work to show us its slow spot. The [mapping note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/business-process-automation-ai) covers the step before any tool, when the job is still a story in someone's head. The [agency note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant) is about hiring, which comes after you know the job. If you hire first, you get sold a stack of tools. The stack was never the real choice.

Owners often tell us they want automation the way a person wants a clean garage. They want the feeling of less mess. That feeling does come, but only after one ugly, repeated job gets a written path to follow. A long menu of features will not bring it.

## What the surveys already count

Statistics Canada found that in the second quarter of 2025, 12.2% of businesses used AI to make goods or deliver services. A year earlier it was 6.1%. (Statistics Canada, 2025) Among the businesses that used AI, 35.7% used text analytics and 23.1% used marketing automation. Also, 40.1% had built new ways of working, and 38.9% had trained their staff. We read that as a list of jobs people tend to start with. We do not read it as a score of how well you are doing. Sorting text shows up, and so does marketing that can be counted. New ways of working and trained people show up right beside the tool, which is the part sellers mention last.

The Chamber's 2025 report says 58% of small businesses use generative AI. That is up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023. (U.S. Chamber of Commerce) It is a different question. Opening a tool that writes text for you is not the same as putting AI inside the way you deliver your product. A shop can sit inside the Chamber number and outside the Statistics Canada number on the same afternoon. If a seller quotes only the bigger share, ask them for the smaller one too. The smaller one is closer to the job you are about to change.

We would read the Statistics Canada list as a plain line of jobs to pick from. You can sort text, run marketing that you can measure, write a new way of working, and train the people who will run it. Try the four-part test on each one before you buy anything. A job that fails the test can still be done by a person. That is not a loss, because it means the test did its work.

## A worked example

Picture the counter of a small company that sells parts to repair shops. This is only a walk-through. We are not claiming a result that we measured. The owner still knows the odd customers by their voices. A bookkeeper posts invoices three mornings a week, and a floor lead pulls the orders. Someone, often the owner's niece, looks after social media, mostly by feeling bad about it.

Three piles sit on the desk, and only one of them deserves a machine.

The invoice pile is dull and never ends. Vendors send scans, and the lines repeat from one scan to the next. The rules are boring and mostly steady. The job is to match the vendor, match the amount, and flag a duplicate. It must never make up a category that the bookkeeper has not approved. A computer can read the scan if it is clear. When it cannot, a person still has the paper. A wrong suggestion only costs a quick fix before anything is posted, as long as the bookkeeper is the one who posts. This pile passes the test, so it is the job we would touch first.

The social pile looks easier, but it is a worse first job than people think. The niece can already write a caption with a tool that makes text. That is the Chamber kind of use, and it is fine. Marketing automation is a real group among the businesses that already use AI, as the Statistics Canada numbers show. Still, it fails our test when nobody knows what a good post is for. It also fails when the product names keep changing because the floor lead hears them wrong. The volume is low and the rules are mushy. A wrong caption is usually cheap to fix, but cheap is not enough when the other parts wobble. We would leave it as a draft that a person writes.

The third pile is a furious one-off. A repair shop says a part failed and wants a credit, a lecture, and a promise. The rules are not steady, because the relationship is the rule. The facts are a phone call, a photo, and ten years of memory in the owner's head. A wrong reply could cost the account. This job fails on purpose, and we would not automate the apology. We would let the owner make it. We would keep the tool away from that thread, so it cannot sound smooth and still be wrong.

We would put the bookkeeper in charge of the invoice test. She knows a duplicate when she sees one, and the niece and the owner do not. The floor lead's job is to say when a vendor name on the scan is the warehouse nickname and not the legal name. The owner's job is to say no when someone wants to add the angry-customer job while they are at it. That refusal is the whole plan.

## How we'd run it

We run the choice like a filter. Anything that gets through can become a small setup. Anything that does not stays manual, and there is no shame in that.

First, we list the possible jobs in the owner's own words on one page, with no tool names. That might be invoices, captions, the angry credit, and a mailbox full of questions about whether you have a certain part. Then we ask which one happens even when everyone is tired, because the tired job is usually the right one. Rare, heroic jobs attract software, and then the software sits unused.

Second, we score each job on the four tests, out loud, with the person who does the work. We ask how often it happens and how steady the rules are. We ask whether a computer can read the source or whether the source is just a memory. We also ask what a wrong answer costs. Can a named person catch it before it leaves? The invoice passes, the caption is a maybe that we set aside, and the credit fails. We write the fails down so they do not creep back into the plan later as a second phase.

Third, we map the job that passed before we look at any products. That map is what the [mapping note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/business-process-automation-ai) is about. We ask who touches the scan and where it is saved. We ask what the bookkeeper changes by hand and what she refuses to let a suggestion decide. If we cannot draw that with her, we are not ready to buy.

… Full post: https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-automation-for-small-business

2. Empowering Small Business Report 2025 — U.S. Chamber of Commerce — https://www.uschamber.com/assets/documents/Empowering-Small-Business-Report-2025.pdf

## AI Consultant for Small Business: What to Ask

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-consultant-for-small-business

A useful consultant names the job, the data, and the stop. Most firms use AI somewhere. Far fewer are scaling agents. Guaranteed rankings are a red flag.

A useful AI consultant for a small business can name the job, the data, and the person who is allowed to stop the work. If a ready-made product already does that job, the honest advice is to buy the product and skip the custom project. We would rather lose the work than invent a build to justify a fee. That is how the [studio](/) works. If you are torn between a consultant and a firm that wants to own the install, read the [agency comparison](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant). If a pretty first test run never became a real process, read the [stall note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/why-ai-pilots-stall).

Bring the person who does the job into the first meeting. An owner alone will be sold a platform. The office manager, the bookkeeper, or the dispatcher will ask where the file lives. That question is worth more than any slide with a diagram. If the consultant looks annoyed by it, you have learned something cheap.

We feel strongly about this because we have watched the other way go wrong. A pitch that starts with a tool name has skipped the work. You can always get back to a tool later. You cannot easily get back the month you spent building the wrong promise.

## What gets canceled

Gartner said in June 2025 that over 40% of AI agent projects will be canceled by the end of 2027. It named cost, unclear business value, and weak risk controls as the reasons. (Gartner, 2025) In a poll of 3,412 people, 19% said their group had made big investments in AI agents. Another 42% had made small ones, 8% had made none, and 31% were waiting or unsure. Gartner also said only about 130 vendors sold what it would call a real AI agent. Think about that last line before you let a proposal use the word agent as decoration. The label is everywhere, but the real thing is rare.

McKinsey's 2025 survey shows the same gap in other numbers. About 88% say they use AI regularly in at least one part of the business, up from 78% a year earlier. (McKinsey) Only 23% are growing an AI agent system somewhere, and 39% are still trying it out. A consultant who quotes only the first number is describing use and not a finished system. Ask them to say the second pair of numbers out loud. If they cannot, they are selling the feeling of being current.

The red flags are easy to spot once you know them. Guaranteed rankings go against Google's own guide. It says the new AI features still depend on ordinary search work. (Google Search Central) Nobody can promise a spot in an AI answer. A person who does will probably bluff on the rest of the job too. If there is no data plan, nobody has named the one place the facts live. If there is no handover, your team cannot run the thing after the last invoice. We treat those three as reasons to end the meeting. We do not treat them as issues to talk through.

## A worked example

Sit in on a hiring talk at a small dental clinic. This is a walk-through we use, and it is not a scoreboard. The owner is a dentist who wants help. The office manager runs the reminders and the front desk, and she is in the room because we asked her to be. The bookkeeper is not there yet. She will matter when the invoice arrives, and she should see the proposal before anyone signs.

The first consultant opens a laptop and names a platform. He talks about AI that will "handle the whole patient journey." He has not asked where the appointment book lives. He has not asked about the paper list of people who do not want texts. When the office manager asks who checks a message before it goes out, he says the system has safety rails. A safety rail is not a name. She writes nothing down, and that is the right instinct.

The second consultant does not open a tool. She asks the office manager to describe last Monday, including the part that went wrong. A reminder went to a patient who was already in the chair, because the reminder list and the treatment list do not talk to each other. The consultant writes one sentence. It says to draft cleaning reminders from the appointment record only, and the office manager sends them. She asks where the do-not-contact names are kept. She asks what happens when the manager is out sick. She also says, out loud, that if a ready-made product already drafts that reminder inside the clinic's software, they should buy it and stop talking to her.

We would hire the second person, and we would still make her put a stop rule in the proposal. The work goes on only if the manager can clear the queue in the time she has set aside. It stops if the drafts keep picking the wrong patients. A consultant who will not write the stop rule is planning to stay forever. That is how a small fee turns into the kind of project Gartner expects many AI agent efforts to cancel.

Notice who did the real interview. It was the office manager, and not the owner. The owner felt the pain, but the manager knows the drawer with the paper list. A good consultant talks to the owner about money and risk. Then she talks to the manager about the Monday. A weak one charms the owner and avoids the manager, since the manager asks questions that shrink the proposal. Let it shrink. A smaller job that is true beats a big job that is foggy.

## How we'd run it

We run a hiring talk like a filter. The consultant is not owed a second meeting.

First, we send our questions ahead in writing, so nobody can say they were ambushed. What job will change? Where does the data live? Who checks the answer, by name? How will we know it failed? What will you refuse to build? If the reply is a calendar link and a slide deck with none of those answers, we skip the meeting. Being polite is not a reason to give away an hour.

Second, we hold the meeting with the person who does the work, and not only the owner. We ask the consultant to say the job in one sentence that the staff could repeat. If the sentence has a tool name in it and no verb the staff would use, we send them back. "Roll out the platform" is not a job. "Draft the cleaning reminder and wait for a person" is a job.

Third, we ask the buy-or-build question straight out, and we watch the face. If a ready-made product already does this, will you say so? The honest answer is yes. It comes with a short list of what they could still help with, such as the wording and the checking step. The dishonest answer is a custom build that copies a feature the clinic's software already sells. It pads the consultant's hours and leaves the manager with two systems to look after.

Fourth, we ask for a handover plan before we talk about price. Who can run this when you leave? Where are the rejected drafts written down? What will the bookkeeper see on the invoice, in words and not only in a total? A price with no handover is really a subscription to one person. That can be fine for advice, but it is a bad way to buy a system.

Sources
1. Over 40 percent of agentic AI projects will be canceled by end of 2027 — Gartner, 2025-06-25 — https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-25-gartner-predicts-over-40-percent-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-canceled-by-end-of-2027
2. The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation — McKinsey — https://www.mckinsey.com/~/media/mckinsey/business%20functions/quantumblack/our%20insights/the%20state%20of%20ai/november%202025/the-state-of-ai-2025-agents-innovation_cmyk-v1.pdf
3. Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search — Google Search Central — https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide

## AI for Small Business: What the Surveys Still Say

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-for-small-business-2027

Two surveys still disagree because they ask different questions. One counts generative AI use. The other counts AI used to produce the goods or the service.

The useful question for a small business is which job actually changes. Two surveys from 2025 are still the clean public counts. They do not measure the same thing. One asks whether a small business uses generative AI. The other asks whether a business used AI to make its goods or deliver its service. You can say yes to the first and no to the second, and be honest both times. If you average them into one "how far behind are we" number, you may buy the wrong project.

We wrote out the full split in the [help note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses). If you want to know what to do about the gap, read the [strategy note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-strategy-for-small-business). If you want to score one firm instead of a whole country, use the [assessment](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-assessment). A survey counts a crowd. Your shop is one set of hands, one set of files, and one job that is slow this week. Start with that job.

People ask us which percentage to believe. We do not treat either one as a verdict on a single owner. What we trust is the wording of the question. If you skip the wording, you can spend a whole season chasing a rank that was never about your counter.

## Two questions, two answers

The Chamber's 2025 report says 58% of small businesses use generative AI, up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023. (U.S. Chamber of Commerce) That question is about using a tool to write a product note, draft a reply, or ask for a checklist. It counts the owner who opened the tool on a Tuesday and got something good enough to edit. It does not ask whether a model made the goods on the shelf. It does not ask whether a model did the work the customer paid for.

Statistics Canada found that 12.2% of businesses used AI to make goods or deliver services in 2025, up from 6.1% a year earlier. (Statistics Canada, 2025) That question is harder and narrower, because it is about the thing you sell. A bakery that uses a tool to write the weekly email can sit inside the Chamber number and outside the Statistics Canada number. A shop where a model suggests orders and a person places them is close to the second question. It may still not meet it. Read the verbs, which are make and deliver. They are not draft, brainstorm, or "we tried it once."

A firm can say yes to the Chamber question and no to the Statistics Canada question. Plan from the job you can name, and do not average the two percentages into one readiness rate. This site does not publish a combined readiness rate, and neither does the Readiness Check. If someone hands you one blended number made from these two, they have glued different questions together.

## A worked example

Walk through a home-goods shop with us. This is an example and not a study, and we are not giving it a score. The owner buys from a few makers and from one wholesaler. A floor lead works the counter and knows which lamp has a chip in the glaze. A bookkeeper comes in part of the week and dislikes surprises in her inbox. The shop has no IT person, and the team talks by group text.

Last winter the owner started using a generative tool for product descriptions. She pastes in a few notes from the maker and asks for a short paragraph in her own voice. Then she edits out anything that sounds like a catalog from nowhere. The floor lead does the same for a social post when a new table arrives. He deletes the line that says the wood is oak when it is not. That is real use, so on the Chamber question this shop says yes.

Nothing about that use makes the lamp or delivers the sale. The owner still picks the maker. The floor lead still wraps the lamp and tells the truth about the chip. He also still calls the customer when the freight is late. The bookkeeper still matches each invoice to the packing slip with her own eyes. On the Statistics Canada question, this shop says no. AI is not making the goods, and it is not doing the work for the customer. Both answers are correct. A consultant who says "you are an AI business now" or "you are behind" has not listened.

Here is a job that might move the shop toward the second question, if they ever want that. The wholesaler's invoices arrive as scans, and the bookkeeper retypes every line. A tool could read each scan and suggest the lines while she still posts them herself. That is closer to the back-office service than a nicer lamp description is. It is still not the shop "running on AI." It is one job with one checker, and it touches work they already do to get paid. We would talk about that job for an hour before we ever mentioned the Chamber number.

The trap in this shop is pride that points the wrong way. The owner feels modern because her descriptions got better. Her nephew told her that most small businesses already do this. He was pointing at the Chamber number without saying what the question was. She also feels secretly behind, because a podcast said only a small slice of firms use AI in production. That podcast was pointing at a number like the Statistics Canada one, again without the question. She is not a laggard and she is not finished. She has a drafting habit and an untouched pile of invoices.

## How we'd run it

We do not start by asking an owner where they rank. We start by pulling the two questions apart, and then we pick one job.

First, we ask what they already open in a normal week. The shop owner will name the writing tool. We write that down as use in the Chamber sense. We do not praise it as a plan, and we do not scold it. A product note that a person edits is a fair use of an afternoon. It is not the same as AI doing the work for the customer.

Second, we ask what the customer pays for and what has to be true for the shop to earn it. In this shop the customer pays for the right object, in the shape the floor lead described. It must be handed over or shipped, with books that explain the invoice. We look for any step in that chain where a model already acts. Usually there is none, and we say so. The Statistics Canada answer stays a no. That is useful, because it stops the owner from bragging about a skill she does not have.

Third, we pick one job that could change the chain. We describe it in a sentence a new hire could follow. For this shop we like the scanned invoice better than the caption. The sentence is to read the wholesaler's scan, suggest the lines, and wait for the bookkeeper to post them. If the owner would rather automate the caption, we will do it. But first she must admit that it does not change delivery. That can still be worth a small habit, but it is not worth a project with a name.

Fourth, we name the checker and the failure. The bookkeeper is the checker. A failure is a line that does not match the packing slip, or a vendor she does not know. If she cannot see the original scan next to the suggestion, the job is not safe. We do not turn it on. This is the same care we give any other install, and a survey cannot do it for her.

… Full post: https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-for-small-business-2027

Sources
1. Empowering Small Business Report 2025 — U.S. Chamber of Commerce — https://www.uschamber.com/assets/documents/Empowering-Small-Business-Report-2025.pdf
2. Analysis in Brief, artificial intelligence use by businesses in Canada — Statistics Canada, 2025-06-16 — https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/11-621-m/11-621-m2025008-eng.htm

## An AI Implementation Framework in Five Stages

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-implementation-framework

Name the job, score the data, write the process, assign a checker, then keep or stop. Surveys show use is common and scaling is not.

An AI implementation framework is the order of work you follow once the job already has a name. NIST calls the risk side of that work Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. (NIST) We use five stages in plain words, because that is how the talk goes when we sit down with an owner. First we name the job. Then we score the data and write the process. After that we pick a checker, and last we keep the work or stop it.

Most small firms we meet are still [partly ready](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/readiness) while those stages are unfinished. A tool is open on someone's laptop and the rest is a hope. A hope is not a stage, and if you skip one you get the stall we describe in the [stall note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/why-ai-pilots-stall). The owner's own read, which should come before any build, is in the [readiness framework](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-framework). This note covers only the order of work after that read exists.

We like a plain, slow order, but most owners like a demo. A demo feels like progress because someone in the room finally relaxes. An order feels like a delay because it is only a list. The list is the work, though, and a framework you cannot walk through on one page is just a brochure. A brochure will not run your business on Monday morning.

## What the numbers say about the middle

McKinsey's 2025 survey says that 88% of people report regular AI use in at least one part of their business. (McKinsey) That is the easy number, and a seller will quote it before the coffee arrives. The harder numbers sit right beside it. An AI agent is a tool that takes actions on its own. Some 23% of companies are rolling out an AI agent system somewhere, while 39% are still trying things out. Among firms that earn less than $100 million, 29% are rolling AI out widely. Among firms that earn more than $5 billion it is nearly half. No more than 10% are rolling out agents in any one part of the business.

If you run a shop, a clinic, or a trades desk, please read that last line slowly. Regular use only means a person opened a tool. Rolling it out in one part of the business means that part runs on a written process, with a person who can stop it. The gap between those two is where projects end up as a browser tab that nobody closes. We do not think a small firm is behind just because it has not rolled out an AI agent system. We think it is right on time if it can finish one job and say honestly who checks the work.

Cisco's 2025 survey of 8,000 leaders found a group called pacesetters, near 13% of that sample. They were 4 times more likely to move a first test run into daily use. (Cisco, 2025) Those leaders work in companies with more than 500 employees. A small business can still copy the order the pacesetters followed, which was to write the process first and then put it to work. You cannot copy their staff or their in-house experts. A test run in that survey is also not the same as a receptionist trying a new inbox on a Tuesday. Take the order they followed and leave the rest behind.

Stop at the stage you cannot finish. If you cannot name a checker, you are not ready to keep the work. We would rather you pause on a page with a name on it. That beats pushing a half-built flow into a week when the office manager is already behind on the phones.

## A worked example

Take a neighborhood dental clinic. We use this walk-through when an owner asks what the stages look like in a real week, and it is not a result we measured. The owner is the dentist, and she still does the exams herself. The office manager runs the schedule and answers the billing questions. She also covers the front desk when someone calls in sick. The front-desk lead answers the phone and sends the reminders. A hygienist knows which patients are in the middle of treatment and which ones only need a cleaning.

The job is narrow. Patients who are due for a cleaning get a short reminder that sounds like the clinic. The dentist does not want a computer booking anything clinical or guessing at a balance. She asks for the reminder message and a person who reads it before it goes out.

We write the job in words the front-desk lead can say out loud. The tool drafts the cleaning reminder from the appointment record and never mentions treatment or a price. A person sends it. If a second job is hiding inside that sentence, we start over. A seller will try to make the job wider in the proposal. This one sentence is how we politely say no.

The data gets scored before anyone connects an account. The appointment book lives in the practice software. A paper list in the manager's drawer names people who asked not to be texted. Insurance notes sit on another screen, and the hygienist knows which patients are upset about a bill. Those sources do not agree with each other. A draft built only from the appointment book would write to someone on the paper list. That mistake shows up on the first Monday if anyone looks.

The process is a chain of hands. On Monday morning the front-desk lead pulls the list of patients who are due, and the draft uses the appointment record only. Anything that sounds like a treatment word goes to the hygienist. The office manager reads the rest and sends it. If she is out, the messages wait, because nobody sends one just because the draft sounded sure of itself.

The checker is the office manager, by name, with time held on her calendar. If she cannot do it, the hygienist is the named backup. A checker who is simply whoever happens to be free is not really a checker at all.

After a few real Mondays, they look at what the manager sent back. If the problems are about wording, they keep the job and tighten the line. If the problems are the wrong people, they stop sending and fix the paper list and the appointment book first. Stopping is a finished stage too. The demo took an afternoon, but the paper list and the rule about waiting took the whole month.

## How we'd run it

We run the stages in order, and we do not open the next one while the current one is still a shrug.

First, we sit with the owner and with one person who does the job by hand. We ask to see last week's work on the screen they really use. Then we write one sentence that names the job, the facts it uses, and the thing the tool must not touch. If they want several jobs, we pick the one that happens every week and hurts when it is late. The rest go on a closed list. Opening that list is how a simple reminder turns into the whole patient experience before anyone has sent a real one.

Second, we score the data in the room. We ask where the record lives, who types it, and what happens when it is wrong. We also ask which other list says something different. In the clinic that is the appointment book against the do-not-text drawer. On a trades desk it is the job ticket against the text thread where the customer changed the light fixture. In a shop it is the register against the note scribbled on the bag.
