3. Cisco AI research: the most AI-ready companies — Cisco, 2025-10-14 — https://newsroom.cisco.com/c/r/newsroom/en/us/a/y2025/m10/cisco-ai-research-the-most-ai-ready-companies-outpace-peers-in-the-race-to-value.html

## AI Readiness Assessment Questionnaire: The Themes

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-assessment-questionnaire

Ask about data, process, people, and the decision before you ask about a tool. A public checklist does not publish a readiness rate for small firms.

An AI readiness questionnaire should bring four themes into the open before anyone names a product. The themes are where the data lives, whether the process is written down, who checks the output, and what a good result would mean. A form that opens with a logo has already skipped the real work.

NIST groups the risk work into four parts, which are Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. (NIST) We are not asking a small firm to build a risk program with those labels on the door. We are asking the questionnaire to cover the same ground in plain speech. Govern is who gets to decide, and Map is what the job really is. Measure is how you would know the output is wrong. And Manage is what you do when it is. A questionnaire that cannot find those four ideas, even in simpler words, is really a sales form.

The [framework](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-framework) is how we score the answers, and the [assessment](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) is the longer reading. The [growth guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/growth) is what the check offers once you have answers. Themes come first, and next steps come after that. A tool comes last, and sometimes it does not come at all.

We like a short questionnaire because length feels thorough and often hides the blank. An owner may answer a long run of soft questions and still not say where the record lives. When that happens, the form has dodged the only question that mattered. We would rather ask four blunt questions that are allowed to be answered with "we do not know."

## What a public checklist does not claim

The AWS checklist for small and midsize businesses, updated in September 2025, walks an owner through readiness questions. (Amazon Web Services, 2025) It does not publish a percentage of businesses that are ready. The OECD SME AI adoption tool, current in 2026, is a self-assessment aid for smaller firms. (OECD) It is not a national adoption rate.

That missing number is the point of this section, so we will not rush past it. Owners often arrive after reading a headline that sounds like a share of firms. They want their questionnaire to end in the same kind of share. Then they can tell a partner that they are above it or below it. Neither of those public pages will give you that share. AWS gives you questions and a way to talk about stages of work. The OECD tool gives a smaller firm a way to check itself. Suppose your questionnaire prints a readiness rate for "businesses like yours" at the bottom. Then ask who was counted, because if the answer is nobody, you are holding a costume.

We still use those pages, but we use them as prompts and not as a league table. The AWS questions help an owner who has only thought about features. And the OECD aid helps a smaller firm that does not want an account or a stored answer. What you leave with is your own set of answers. You do not leave with permission to say that a percentage of your industry is ready. And we will not write that sentence for you because the sources will not write it either.

Ask where the one place the facts live is for the job. Ask which step is written down and which step is only habit. Ask who can reject the output, and ask what you will stop doing if the answer is weak. Those four questions are the questionnaire.

Say them in the language of the job, or they stay abstract. The question "Where do the facts live?" becomes a plainer one about a real call. When a customer calls about the thing we promised, which page does the person on the phone open? The question about habit becomes a different one. What do we do when the usual person is out, and is that written anywhere a new hire could find? The question about rejecting becomes a third one. Who is allowed to say that this message does not go to the customer? Then the question about what we will stop becomes a last one. If this works, which notebook can we close for good?

A questionnaire that cannot survive that translation is still just a theme list. Themes are not a score, because they are the questions you refuse to skip. We send people to the growth guide once real answers exist. By then the next move is about getting better at the job and not about collecting more questions. Please do not open that guide to avoid the four questions, and open it only after you have answers you can stand behind.

We also want the questionnaire to record disagreement. If the owner and the person who does the job give different answers, the form should show both and not a negotiated average. An average is how a blank turns into a tick. Write "owner says the binder, dispatcher says her head" and leave it ugly. Ugly is honest. A clean tick that needed a compromise in the hallway is how you buy a tool for a process that does not exist.

NIST's four words help us check that we did not drift into product trivia. If the questionnaire never asks who decides, it skipped Govern. And if it never asks what the job is in steps a stranger could follow, it skipped Map. If it never asks how you would notice a wrong output, it skipped Measure. And if it never asks what you will do when the output is wrong, it skipped Manage. You can fail all four tests with a very professional-looking form, and we have watched it happen. The form had sections and a logo but nowhere to write "we do not know."

## A worked example

Say we are at the desk of a small electrical contractor in the late afternoon, when the phones have finally gone quiet. There is an owner, a dispatcher, and a lead who actually walks the jobs. This is an example we walk through, and it is not a firm we audited. We are not going to pretend that we counted their jobs.

The owner was handed a questionnaire by a software seller. It opened with the product name and asked how many users she might want, whether she liked dashboards, and how soon she could start. None of that is a readiness question, so we set it aside and ask our four.

Where do the facts live for a booked job? The owner says the job system. The dispatcher says he keeps a whiteboard because the system is wrong by the time a customer changes a time. The lead says she trusts the text the dispatcher sends her in the morning, because the whiteboard and the system have both let her down. That gives us three answers, and the questionnaire does not get to average them. The one place the facts live is still unresolved, and that unresolved state is the answer we write down.

Which step is written, and which step is habit? The written step is the quote, and the owner is proud of the quote template, as she should be. The habit is everything that happens after the customer says yes. Who tells the lead about the parking note, and who calls the customer when a part slips? Who decides that a job is done enough to invoice? The dispatcher says "we just do it." The lead says she calls the owner when she is unsure, and that means the owner's phone is the process.

… Full post: https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-assessment-questionnaire

2. AI readiness checklist for small and midsize businesses — Amazon Web Services, 2025-09-01 — https://aws.amazon.com/smart-business/resources-for-smb/ai-readiness-checklist/
3. OECD SME AI adoption tool — OECD — https://sme.oecd.ai/

## AI Readiness Assessment: What It Measures and How to Score

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-assessment

An AI readiness assessment looks at data, process, people, and decisions. Compare the public tools, then see what our Readiness Check gives you.

An AI readiness assessment asks whether a business can put a new tool to work. Public indexes and checklists answer that question for different groups of people. The groups are easy to mix up. This note compares them. Then it explains what the [Readiness Check guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/readiness) looks at for the firm that is actually in the room.

We get asked for "our number," as if readiness were a credit score you could borrow from a headline. A figure about leaders at big companies cannot tell a clinic whether the front desk and the clinician use the same record.

## What the public tools measure

Cisco put out its third yearly AI Readiness Index on 14 October 2025. It surveyed 8,000 senior leaders at companies with more than 500 employees. Those leaders came from 30 markets and 26 industries. (Cisco, 2025) The leaders it calls pacesetters stayed near 13% of the sample for three years. Those companies were 4 times more likely to turn a first trial into real use. They were also 50% more likely to see real value. Of all the people surveyed, 83% plan to use AI agents. Nearly 40% expect agents to work beside staff within a year. That sample is not a small-business survey.

Owners hear the Cisco line on a podcast and wonder if they are behind. Behind what, and compared with whom? They would be behind a company big enough to put a senior leader on a survey. The 13% figure is a fair check for large firms. It is a poor mirror for a practice with a front desk and two treatment rooms.

One part still fits a small firm, and that is the gap between a trial and daily work. The companies that cross that gap have the job written down. The demo was never the hard part. So if you use Cisco at all in a small firm, use it as a warning against mistaking a trial for a habit. Please do not use it as a ranking that you are supposed to join.

Gartner said on 26 February 2025 that 63% of the people it asked do not have the data habits that AI needs. Some of them were also not sure they had those habits. (Gartner, 2025) The same note predicts that through 2026, companies will give up on 60% of AI projects that lack data made ready for AI. We point to that line when someone wants to skip the record and start with a login. The project stops when the data was never ready. That story is not hard to guess.

The OECD tool for small and midsize firms is a short self-check about AI use. It is part of the work of the 2026 French Group of Seven Presidency. (OECD) It takes about five minutes and stores no data. Your answers stay in the browser. As of May 2026 it is a test version, and Group of Seven governments are still checking it. It does not publish an adoption rate. We like it as a set of questions you can answer without making an account. We do not like it as a stand-in for a national share, because it never claims to be one.

AWS posted an AI readiness checklist in September 2025. (Amazon Web Services, 2025) It walks through five steps and sorts a business into four stages. The stages run from Not yet ready, through Emerging and Operational, to a last stage about using AI widely. They cover the data, the use case, the tools, the rules, and the numbers you will watch. The page does not cite an adoption percentage. Stages are plain descriptions that you can argue with. A percentage that nobody counted is just a rumor with a percent sign.

Here is a plain comparison of who each tool describes and what you leave with.

- Cisco's index describes companies with more than 500 employees, so you get a comparison with pacesetters and not a score for one small firm.
- The OECD tool describes the smaller firms in the Group of Seven test, so you get a short self-check that stays in the browser.
- The AWS checklist describes a small or midsize business, so you get five steps and four stage names.
- The Readiness Check describes the business taking it, so you get next steps for your business and three tips for each section.

The Readiness Check is the one built for the firm in the room. It teaches and points the way, but it does not diagnose. We publish the method on [our site](/).

We draw that line on purpose. A diagnosis says what is wrong with you. A route says where to look next. Owners sometimes want the diagnosis because it sounds more serious, but serious is not the same as useful. If we told a clinic that it had failed readiness, we would be borrowing a doctor's tone for a business talk. The check describes where you stand and points to a next page. That is the promise we make.

## What the check gives you

The Readiness Check asks about the same four parts as this note. (Abracadabra AI) It gives you next steps for your business. The step depends on where the work stands today.

- If the work that matters still lives in people's heads, the first useful step is to write one job down and name who owns it.
- If parts of the work are written down, a named owner and one place for the facts can turn that into something a team can run.
- If the business can put a new tool to work, the open question is which job to start with and who owns it day to day.
- If a real job already uses the tools, the next gain is the job that still waits on one person.

A next step tells you where to look today, and it is not a grade. The check takes five to seven minutes with one question on each screen. It gives three tips for each section.

When the know-how is still in people's heads, you write one job down and name the owner before you shop. When the writing is only partial, two pieces are often missing. One is a named owner, and the other is one place where the facts live. Without them nobody else can run the job when the usual person is out.

When a new tool can land, the argument left is which job goes first and who lives with it on an ordinary day. When a real job already uses the tools, the gain left is the job that still waits on one person. Everyone goes around that job because it is "easier to ask her."

People hear an early step as a scolding, but we do not. A first step is a clear description, and it is often the honest one. A clinic can be excellent at care and still be new to the paperwork around recalls. Those are different skills. The step is about whether a tool has anything solid to stand on. It is not a review of the owner's character.

The next note looks at [how surveys count AI in small businesses](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses). That is a different question from whether one firm is ready. A survey can talk about firms in general. It cannot say whether your front desk and your clinician agree on the chart note. We try not to let the wide question answer the narrow one.

## A worked example

Say we are in a small physiotherapy clinic after the last patient has gone home. One person runs the front desk. One clinician sees most of the repeat visits. This is an example we walk through, and it is not a clinic we measured.

## AI Readiness Checklist Before You Buy a Tool

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-checklist

Questions to answer before you buy an AI tool, grouped by data, process, people, and the decision. Public surveys name the gaps those questions catch.

An AI readiness checklist is the list of questions you answer before you pay for a tool. We use it when an owner has a demo booked. The owner has not yet said which job the tool is for. The questions fall into four groups, which are data, process, people, and the decision. A vendor's feature list cannot stand in for any of them.

The [Readiness Check](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check) asks about the same four groups, and it gives you next steps for your business. The [assessment note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) compares the public tools, and the [data note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-ready-data) stays on the first group. If the process is your weak spot, the [process guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-process-low) is the page we hand over.

We think of the checklist as a brake. The tour of a tool always looks tidy. The real test comes on the busy afternoon after it, when nobody remembers which screen is the right one. A tick means you can point to the answer, and a blank means you cannot. The blanks are the useful part.

## Data and process

Here are the questions for the first two groups. Can you name the one place the facts live for this job? Is it current, and can a system read it without someone retyping it? Is the job written down, including the exceptions, and does one person own the handoff?

We ask these out loud. The person who does the work must be in the room, and not only the person who signs the check. The owner answers from memory, and the person at the counter answers from last Thursday. When the two disagree, the list has already paid for itself.

Every shop we sit in has more than one place where a fact can live. There is the notebook, the spreadsheet the bookkeeper trusts, the supplier portal, and the text thread. The record you mean is whichever one the next person will believe when they disagree. If you cannot name that one, a new tool just becomes another place to hunt.

Next we ask whether the record is current and whether a system can read it. A record that gets patched from memory is more of a souvenir than a source. For an open order, current means the status changed when the part came in. It does not mean someone updated it after they remembered to call. If someone still has to retype the record, the tool will wait on that person. Retyping is the job you have not replaced yet.

The process questions sit beside the data questions because a clean record with no written handoff will still stall. We want the happy path and the exceptions too. What happens when the part is wrong? What if the customer does not answer, or the usual person is out? If those live only as habit, the tool will follow the happy path and make up the rest. One person has to own the handoff, even on the day that person is out. A handoff that everyone owns tends to belong to no one.

In February 2025, Gartner reported that 63% of respondents do not have the data practices that AI needs, or are not sure they do. (Gartner, 2025) The same note says that through 2026 companies will abandon 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data. We read that as a reason to treat the data questions as the main event. A large firm and a small counter can fail the same way. The record is not ready, and the project dies once the demo fades.

AWS published a checklist in September 2025. (Amazon Web Services, 2025) It walks through five steps. It sorts a business into four stages, called Not yet ready, Emerging, Operational, and Scaling. The page does not cite an adoption percentage, and we like that. A stage name is a description you can argue with. If a page will not say how many firms it counted, do not turn its silence into a rate.

We use those stage names as labels and not as a grade. Not yet ready means the job still lives in one person's head. Emerging means some of it is written down while a lot of it is habit. Operational means your staff can run the job without a hero. Scaling means you repeat a pattern instead of finding it. You do not have to adopt the labels, but you do have to say which one fits.

We open the process guide when this half of the list is mostly blank. We fix the writing before we fix the software. A short written handoff, with the exceptions on the same page, beats a tool that thinks the handoff is already there.

## People and the decision

Who may use a tool, and who may send its output to a customer? Those are the people questions, and they are where checklists tend to go soft. "Everyone will use it" is not an answer. A name is an answer, and so is a rule about what can leave the building.

Microsoft's 2024 Work Trend Index says 75% of knowledge workers use AI at work. It says 46% of those users started less than six months earlier. (Microsoft WorkLab, 2024) It also says 78% of AI users bring their own tools, and at small and midsize companies that share is 80%. It also says 60% of leaders worry that their company's leadership lacks a plan and vision to put AI in place.

In a small company those figures show up as one person. Someone is already pasting notes into a personal account because the official way is slow. They are only trying to finish the day. A checklist that never asks who brought a tool in will miss the real system. That system is often the one in a coat pocket.

We ask who uses the tool on a normal day. We ask who may send its words to a customer. We also ask who can stop it when it is wrong. If nobody can stop it, you do not have a people plan. You have a hope that the errors will be obvious.

The decision questions are separate. What would count as success, who can stop the experiment, and what happens if the tool is wrong? "Sam will keep an eye on it" names a person. "The customer hears from the record, not from memory" is a decision. So is "if it sends a wrong message, we turn it off the same day." We write each one on its own line.

A tick list does not tell you which gap is largest. The Readiness Check asks about the same four groups and gives you next steps for your business. We still want the paper list first. A next step without a talk is easy to skip. The list is the talk. The check is what you use when you want the same questions asked the same way next time.

When the room is being polite, we add one more decision question. What will you stop doing if this works? If the answer is nothing, the tool is a hobby. The checklist is allowed to end with a no. A no that names the blank box is a better result than a yes that names a logo.

## A worked example

Say we are sitting after close with the owner of a neighborhood hardware shop. A counter lead and a bookkeeper are there too. This is an example we walk through, and it is not a report of a shop we measured.

The owner wants a tool that drafts the message saying a special order is in. It would also suggest which supplier to chase. The demo was slick, but the checklist is the part where we ignore the demo.

We start with data.

## An AI Readiness Framework an Owner Can Score

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-framework

Score data, process, people, and the decision in words. Public research names the gaps. The Readiness Check gives you next steps for your business.

An AI readiness framework is a way to score the business before you score a tool. We use it when an owner wants a plan and all anyone has offered is a product tour. The tour can wait, because the score is about the work.

NIST groups AI risk work as Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. (NIST) This note uses four groups an owner can see, which are data, process, people, and the decision. We call each group absent, partial, in place, or running. Those words are anchors and not a percentage. If you cannot point at the thing, you do not get the stronger word. We would rather call data absent than call it running because the owner feels modern.

The [readiness guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/readiness) is the matching page. The [assessment](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) is the longer note, and the [questionnaire](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-assessment-questionnaire) is the list of questions. The framework is what you do with the answers once they are on paper. You do not turn them into a fake share of readiness. You give each group a word you can defend.

## What the check adds

The Readiness Check asks about the same four groups. (Abracadabra AI) It gives you next steps for your business. The check helps you see where to look next. It does not certify a business.

Read the result as a shape and not as a medal. Sometimes the work that matters still lives in people's heads. Sometimes some of it is written down, but nobody clearly owns it. Sometimes you could put a system on the job without making up the job at the same time. And sometimes the tools already do real work, and the leftover pain is the task everyone still hands to one person. A result without those sentences is just a label. We do not certify anyone with it, because certifying is what a buyer wants to wave at a board. A small firm has no such board, and we will not pretend the check is a seal.

Gartner said in February 2025 that 63% of respondents do not have, or are unsure they have, the data practices AI needs. (Gartner, 2025) Through 2026, companies will abandon 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data. A framework that scores data as running while the facts sit in a shared inbox is scoring a wish. We keep that idea in the room during the talk. The research is about the people Gartner asked and not about your shop. It still describes the failure we watch, where the project looks alive until the record has to carry it.

Cisco's 2025 index surveyed 8,000 senior leaders at companies with more than 500 employees. (Cisco, 2025) The leaders it called pacesetters were near 13%, and their companies were 4 times more likely to move a pilot into production. That group is not a small business. The pattern still matters, because production follows a written process and not a demo. If you quote the 13% at a bakery and call the baker not a pacesetter, you have changed the group. The framework helps us avoid that slide. We score the bakery in words, and we do not borrow a big-company league table.

Score the four groups in words first. Then take the check if you want next steps. Words come first because a label is easy to flatter. If you jump to the label, you will argue with it and not with the inbox.

Here is how we pick the words, so they do not turn into moods. Data is absent when nobody can name the record. It is partial when a record exists, but people keep a side copy they trust more. It is in place when one current record is the one a new person would open, and a system could read it without anyone retyping it. It is running when that record already feeds a job you do every week, and someone notices when a field is wrong.

Process is absent when the steps live in one person's head. It is partial when the usual path is written down and the exceptions are folklore. It is in place when the exceptions sit on the same page and one person owns the handoff, even on the day they are out. It is running when everyone follows that page without a meeting to find it again.

People is absent when nobody has said who may send output to a customer, and nobody has noticed that someone already does. It is partial when use is casual and nobody knows who can say no. It is in place when a named person may use the tool, a named person may send, and a named person may stop it. It is running when that stop has been used at least once and not just promised.

The decision is absent when success means less chaos. It is partial when success has a name but nobody can end the trial. It is in place when success, the person who can stop it, and the rule for wrong output are all written as sentences. It is running when you have already stopped something because the rule said to. A decision that has never met a bad week is still a draft.

The check sits on top of those words and does not replace them. Its next steps point you somewhere, and the four words tell you where to work. We have watched owners cheer for a good result and ignore data that was still partial. The framework makes that cheer walk past the weak group first.

## A worked example

Say we are in a small bakery after the morning rush. One person runs the front, and another runs the kitchen and the special-order book. This is an example we walk through, and it is not an audit. We did not measure their flour, and we will not invent a before and after.

The owner wants a tool that answers catering emails and suggests a quote. The demo replied faster than the front lead can. The framework is the part where we ignore the speed and score the job.

First, data. The special-order book is a paper notebook in the kitchen. The front lead also keeps notes in the shop inbox, because customers write to the shop address. The owner has a price sheet that is mostly current. We ask which record a quote must match, and the three of them do not agree. So data is absent for the catering job, even though a notebook exists. A notebook that nobody treats as final is not the one place the facts live. Calling it in place because paper feels solid would be the wish Gartner warns about, where the project is dropped later because the data was never ready. We say absent.

Next, process. The usual path is real. An email comes in, the kitchen lead checks the book, the owner sets a price, and the front lead replies. The exception is a customer who changes the head count the day before, or a date the kitchen lead half promised on the phone. Nobody wrote that down, so process is partial. The usual path is not the whole process. If we scored it in place, the tool would invent the head count change and sound sure about it.

Then people. The front lead already drafts replies in a personal account when she falls behind, and then she pastes them into the inbox. The owner did not know that customer words were being drafted somewhere else. Nobody is named as the person who may send, and nobody is named as the person who may block a send.

4. Cisco AI research: the most AI-ready companies — Cisco, 2025-10-14 — https://newsroom.cisco.com/c/r/newsroom/en/us/a/y2025/m10/cisco-ai-research-the-most-ai-ready-companies-outpace-peers-in-the-race-to-value.html

## AI-Ready Data: What a Small Business Needs First

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-ready-data

AI-ready data means one current source for the job, readable by a system. Gartner's figures describe the firms that do not have that yet.

AI-ready data for a small business is one current place a system can read. It also needs a person who knows which fields are wrong. It is not a warehouse, a lake, or a platform with a serious name. If the answer lives only in someone's head, the tool will make up a second version. That version will sound very sure of itself.

Owners often hear that they must "get their data ready," as if that meant hiring consultants. It sounds like you must also buy a new place to store everything. For the job in front of you, ready means something much smaller. You need one place for the facts. It has to be current enough that the person doing the job trusts it today. A system has to be able to read it without anyone retyping it. And someone has to know which fields look fine but are not. If you cannot point at that place, stop the purchase.

The [low-data guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-data-low) and the [mid-data guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-data-mid) are the matching fixes. The [checklist](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-checklist) asks the same question before you buy anything. Low means you cannot yet name the place the facts live. Mid means you have something, but a system should not trust it yet. Neither guide is a shopping list.

## What the research counts

Gartner reported in February 2025 that 63% of respondents lack the data management practices AI needs, or are unsure they have them. (Gartner, 2025) It also said that through 2026, firms will abandon 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data. We do not cite the sample size here, because the article and its structured data do not agree on it.

We keep that last point because it is easy to turn a percentage into more precision than it has. The 63% is what the note reports about the people it asked. We will not add a sample size that the page does not let us stand behind. The useful part is the shape of the failure. Firms go ahead without the practices, and then they drop the projects. A tool can be full of features and still be unsupported if the record under it is a guess.

A later Gartner article is from January 2026. It says at least 50% of generative AI projects were abandoned after the first test run by the end of last year. (Gartner, 2026) The reasons it gives are poor data quality, weak risk controls, rising costs, and unclear business value.

Read those reasons as ways a first test run can flatter you. The demo works on a clean slice that someone prepared by hand. Poor data quality shows up when the real record arrives, with blank fields and two spellings of the same customer. Weak risk controls show up when nobody is allowed to stop a wrong answer. Rising costs show up when the retyping you hoped to delete is still there. Now there is a new fee too. Unclear value shows up when you cannot say what you stopped doing. The figure for abandoned projects describes work that looked like a success once. So it is a good reason to refuse a test that uses better data than you really have.

| Where the knowledge lives | What a tool can do with it |
| --- | --- |
| Only in one person's head | Almost nothing that can be repeated |
| In documents that no system can read | A person still has to retype it all |
| In one system with a current record | The job can be tried |

Pick one job and name the place its facts live. If you cannot, stop the purchase and fix that first. That is the whole data test.

The table is the test, and owners often answer it with a tour of their software instead of a location. If the knowledge lives in one person's head, a tool has almost nothing it can repeat. If it lives in documents no system can read, a person still retypes, which means you bought a second job. If it lives in one system with a current record, the job can be tried. Tried is the honest word, because the table does not promise success. It only says the attempt is no longer make-believe.

We add one more question in conversation that the table does not need to print. It is who knows which fields are wrong. A current record can still flatter you. The phone number may be right while the box that says "approved for the extra work" is only wishful. The person who knows that is part of AI-ready data. A warehouse without that person is just a larger place to be wrong.

There are two phrases we will not accept in place of a named place for the facts. "We have a lot of data" means a pile, and a pile is not kept current on purpose. "We can export it" means a person can make a snapshot that starts going stale while the file downloads. An export is a document. If no system can read the live record, you are in the middle row of the table. The person who exports it has become the process. Fix the place they export from before you call the export a plan.

## A worked example

Say we are in the office of a small landscaping company on a weekday morning. One person does the scheduling and another leads a crew. This is an example we walk through, so we are not reporting their routes or their revenue. There is no measured before and after, only a job and a question about where its record lives.

The job the owner wants a tool to do is the customer update. It says what the crew did, what is left, and whether the customer owes a decision about extra work. A vendor showed a draft that sounded like the crew lead, only smoother. The owner liked the sound, so we asked where the facts in that draft would come from.

The scheduler says the booking tool is the answer, because it knows the address and the time window. The crew lead says the truth is in the note she writes in a group text. She sends it after the crew walks the yard. The owner keeps a spreadsheet of who has approved extras. He does not trust the booking tool with money questions. That makes three homes for one update. A draft built from the booking tool alone will miss the yard note and may invent the approval. The made-up version will sound like the crew lead. It will be wrong in the way that costs trust.

Using the words of the table, the knowledge lives partly in one person's head until she sends her text. That head is the crew lead's. It also lives in documents the booking tool does not read, which are the group text and the owner's spreadsheet. It does not yet live in one system with a current record of the whole job. A system could read the address. It could not read "the side bed was wetter than expected, so we stopped and need a yes on the extra drainage." That only works if someone retypes it into a field. So the middle row is the honest row, because a person still has to retype. Buying the draft tool now adds a voice to the retyping and does not remove it.

We then ask who knows which fields are wrong. The crew lead knows the yard, and the scheduler knows which customers answer their phones. The owner knows his spreadsheet falls behind whenever he is out on a job himself.

… Full post: https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-ready-data

1. Lack of AI-ready data puts AI projects at risk — Gartner, 2025-02-26 — https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-02-26-lack-of-ai-ready-data-puts-ai-projects-at-risk
2. Why generative AI projects fail after proof of concept — Gartner, 2026-01-26 — https://www.gartner.com/en/articles/genai-project-failure

## AI Strategy for Small Business: Start With the Job

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-strategy-for-small-business

Name the job, the data, and who checks the output before you buy a tool. Use is already common. A written plan and staff training are not.

An AI plan for a small business is a short list you can say out loud. It names the job that changes, the facts it needs, and the person who checks the work. It is not a list of tools, and it is not a big speech about the future. If your page cannot name those three things, you have a pile of apps and a hope that the pile will turn into a plan.

The [assessment](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) scores the same groups of facts we want on that page. The [implementation framework](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-implementation-framework) is the order of work once the job has a name. The [readiness framework](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-framework) is the score sheet under both of them. We start with the job. The tools can wait in the other room until the page exists.

We have watched owners skip the page because it felt too small to matter. In a company this size, a good plan is one job that still works in a busy week. A thick binder that covers every department you do not have is just for show.

## Use is ahead of the plan

Microsoft's 2024 Work Trend Index says 75% of knowledge workers use AI at work. (Microsoft WorkLab, 2024) Of those users, 46% started less than six months before the survey. Also, 60% of leaders worry that their company has no clear plan for how to use AI. About 78% of AI users bring their own tools to work. At small and midsize businesses, that goes up to 80%.

Leaders also worry about finding talent, and 55% said so. Yet only 25% of companies were planning to offer training on generative AI. We read that as a truck cab and a front office that have not met yet. People already use the tools. But the plan, the training, and the hiring worries are all behind them.

NIST's risk framework groups the work into four parts called Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. (NIST) A plan that cannot point to those four parts has not really started. Govern means who is allowed to decide. Map means where the work and the facts live. Measure means how you will know when the answer is wrong. Manage means what you do in the week it is wrong. If your page is only a list of product names, it skips all four.

Salesforce asked 3,350 leaders at firms with 200 workers or fewer. (Salesforce, 2024) The survey ran in August and September 2024. About 75% said they were at least trying out AI, and that rose to 83% among growing small and midsize businesses. Among growing firms, 78% planned to spend more on AI. Only 55% of the firms that were shrinking did. Of the leaders who already used AI, 91% said it helps their revenue. Those are leaders talking about their own companies, so we will not repeat the claim as if your revenue had already agreed.

These numbers come from different groups of people. Microsoft asked knowledge workers and leaders, while Salesforce asked small business leaders. Neither one can take the place of a job you can name on a single page. A worker who brings a tool from home and a leader who says revenue went up can both be telling the truth. They are just answering different questions. Your page still has to pick one job.

## A worked example

Picture a heating and cooling company that runs a handful of trucks. This is only an example, and nobody measured it for a report. The owner prices jobs from the driver's seat. He has started pasting notes about a broken unit into a chatbot on his own phone. He likes the draft it gives him, but he has not told the dispatcher.

The dispatcher builds the day's board from calls, texts, and a whiteboard that is more right than the software they pay for. Two techs trust the board. They do not trust a long message the owner forwards at night.

So there is no plan yet, just people quietly using their own tools. That is the same habit we saw in the Microsoft numbers, where most AI users bring their own tools and even more do at small and midsize businesses. The owner is not a bad guy. He found something that helps him write a quote when he is tired. The trouble starts when a customer reads the draft back to the dispatcher the next morning. It names a part the shop does not stock and a price the owner would have changed at a desk.

The office manager finds out in the worst way, which is from the customer. She has no page that says which jobs the tool may touch. She has no rule that a quote only leaves after she or the dispatcher has seen it. Nobody trained her, because there was nothing to train on except that the boss has an app. The low training numbers from Microsoft will sound familiar to her. She lives in the gap between using the tool and having a plan.

Here is the page we would write with them, and it still has no tool name on it. The job is to draft estimates for swap-out jobs. It is not for complaints or anything that sounds like a safety problem. The facts come from the price book on the office computer and the notes the tech already puts on the ticket. They do not come from the owner's memory of a house that looked similar. The dispatcher checks the draft, because she already knows which crews can do the work this week. When she is out, the office manager takes her place, and both names are written down. If a draft names a part they do not stock, it does not go out. That is a real plan, and it is short enough to tape inside a cabinet door.

We also left some things off the page on purpose. We did not write that the company will look for ways to use AI everywhere. We did not put a chatbot on the website. The techs need the board to stay right. The owner's late night drafts can stay only if they become drafts the dispatcher expects, built from facts the office already trusts. Until then, the honest rule is to stop forwarding the chat to customers.

## How we'd run it

We build the page before we add a login, because the order matters more than the paperwork.

First, we ask the owner what he already does in private. The chatbot in the truck is a fact, so we write it down and we do not scold him for it. We call it bring-your-own use, which is common. We keep it apart from a company plan, which is not. A habit that stays hidden is risky. But once we name it, we can change it.

Second, we pick one job and draw a fence around it. Swap-out estimates are inside the fence. Complaints, safety calls, and anything the price book cannot back up are outside it. The fence is the plan. A job with no fence turns into every job by Friday, because the tool will answer any question you type. Being able to answer is not the same as having permission.

Third, we name the facts and the checker in the same meeting. For this company the price book and the ticket notes are in, and the owner's memory is out. The dispatcher checks, and the office manager covers. We put time on the dispatcher's calendar so that checking is a real slot and not just a good idea. This is where the Map and Measure parts of the NIST framework live, even if we never say those words in the room.

2. AI risk management framework — NIST — https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework

## Answer Engine Optimization: What Google Still Requires

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/answer-engine-optimization

Google still treats answer-engine work as ordinary SEO. A research paper reports visibility gains. Pew found fewer clicks when a summary appears.

Answer engine optimization is the work of getting cited when an AI writes an answer. Google still treats that work as ordinary search work, so the new name does not give your site a new set of rules.

Google's guide says the work is still the same old search work. (Google Search Central) The page has to be in Google's list of pages, and it has to be able to show a snippet, which is the short piece of text Google puts under a result. Google says it does not use llms.txt, which is a plain file some people add to a site to tell AI tools what to read. It also says there is no special way you must cut up your text. And no extra hidden labels in the page code are needed for these features. We turn that into a short list of things you do not get. You do not get a magic file that makes you the answer. You do not get to hide the real page behind a block of text a person cannot read. What you do is plain. You publish a page Google can list, a page a snippet can lift from, and a page a customer can finish.

The [visibility guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/visibility) is the matching check for whether the site can be cited at all. The [ChatGPT note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/how-to-get-your-business-to-show-up-in-chatgpt) covers crawler files, which are a different switch from this one. The [GEO comparison](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/generative-engine-optimization-vs-seo) puts the research and the click study side by side, if you want to see both.

## What the research measured

A 2024 paper on generative engine optimization reports visibility gains of up to 40%. (arXiv, 2024) Methods that add citations, quotes, and facts with numbers were linked to gains of more than 40%. On Perplexity, which is an AI search tool, the gain reached 37%. A score for how much of the answer came from the page rose 41%, and a score for how useful the answer felt rose 28%. The test used ten thousand questions. Those results come from pages written to be easier for an AI answer to lift from. They do not promise that your faucet page will move by a set amount because you added a quote.

When we sit with an owner, we take one thing from the paper. It is the kind of sentence that got the lift. A citation points at a source. A quote is a real person saying something you can check. A number with a clear group behind it is a fact the answer can carry. A page that says "we are the best hardware store in town" has none of those. A better page says how a cartridge is measured, quotes the maker's note on fit, and tells the reader which handles in the aisle match it. The gain is tied to that kind of writing. It is not tied to the phrase "answer engine" in the footer.

Pew, in July 2025, found that people clicked a link 8% of the time when an AI summary showed up. (Pew Research Center, 2025) When no summary showed up, they clicked 15% of the time. A citation that nobody clicks is still a citation. But you should write the page so the click is worth taking.

Owners feel that drop at the till, even if they never see the study. If the summary already told the person the cartridge size, they may not need you for that fact. They still need you for the part in stock and the person who will show them the wrench. They also need an honest line about what you will not do on a Sunday. Put that on the page. The summary can borrow the size, but the visit is for the counter.

## A worked example

Walk into a hardware store on your street. This is an example we talk through, and it is not a result. One person works the counter and knows which aisle has what. People already ask a question like this, out loud and in search: can someone cut a key and tell me which cartridge fits my dripping faucet?

The old page says the store sells hardware, paint, and keys. It has a phone number and a cheerful line about friendly service. Google barely lists it, and a snippet would have nothing sharp to lift. An AI asked about that faucet will cite a page that states the size, the common mix-up, and what to bring to the counter. The owner's page can be that page. But it will not get there by adding a new acronym to the title.

What the counter lead knows is the raw material. He already tells the person holding a bag of old parts that the stem length matters more than the brand on the handle. He also says a photo of the old cartridge saves a second trip. That line belongs at the top, in words a summary can quote and a person can use. Under it, the owner writes what the store really does. They cut keys while you wait on the days the counter lead is in. They match cartridges if you bring the old one or a clear photo. They do not fix pipes inside the wall. That last line is useful because it keeps the answer honest. It also keeps a click from turning into a sad visit.

Each person has a clear job. The owner owns the claims and will not let the page say they repair what they only sell. The counter lead checks the draft against what he says at the counter, because a polished sentence that does not match him will annoy the next customer. Whoever updates the site, even if that is a nephew, has one job. The page must stay listed, the first sentences must answer the question, and the source of any number must be easy to see. If a number is about their own stock, the page says it is theirs. If it comes from a maker's sheet, the page names the sheet. That is the same move as the paper's citations and quotes, done at the size of one shop.

An AI answer might then say the stem length matters and send the person to the owner. Pew's finding is why the page cannot stop at the fact the summary will take. The summary can explain the stem, but the page has to make the trip better. Bring the old cartridge. The counter lead is the one who matches it. The store does not open the wall. Those lines are the reason to click, and they also keep the citation from turning into a complaint.

## How we'd run it

We would not start with a tool that "does answer engine work." We would start with the page a customer already lands on, and we would ask whether a stranger could act on it.

First, we check that the page is in Google's list and can show a snippet. If it is blocked, thin, or tucked behind a form, we stop there. Google's guide is blunt that these features still need an ordinary page. No special file can take the place of one.

Second, we write the question in the customer's own words at the top, and we answer it in the next sentences. That might be key cutting, a cartridge match, or what to bring. A heading that repeats the question helps a person scan the page, and it gives an answer something clean to lift. This is plain structure and not a special ritual. Google says it has no special rule for how you cut up the text.

Third, we add the kind of material the 2024 paper linked to the gains. That means a real citation, a real quote, and a real number.

3. Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears — Pew Research Center, 2025-07-22 — https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears/

## Business Process Automation With AI: Write the Job

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/business-process-automation-ai

Write the steps before you add a model. Most knowledge workers already use AI. Few companies were planning training. Many proofs of concept still stop.

Business process automation with AI starts with a written job. We mean the steps a person already follows, in order. We also mark the spot where they use their own judgment. An AI model can't follow a job that lives in someone's head. It will make up the missing steps, and the made-up steps will sound very sure of themselves. Anthropic's December 2024 essay says to start with the simplest thing that works. It also says to keep a fixed list of steps until the next step truly depends on what the last one found. (Anthropic, 2024) We treat that as everyday advice. The tool comes after the page, and if the page is blank, the tool is just guessing.

If the steps are not written down, stop spending money. The [process guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-process-mid) is the matching fix for that blank page. The [automation note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-automation-for-small-business) helps you pick which job to start with once you can see more than one. The [agents note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-agents-for-business) covers a later question. It asks what to do when a fixed list is not enough, because the next step depends on what the last step found. An AI agent is a tool that picks its own next step. Most of the rooms we sit in are not ready for that yet. People are still telling the work from memory, and the story changes each time we ask.

## The process is the product

The map is the thing you are making. Software is only a way to run that map the same way on a busy Tuesday as on a quiet Monday. Microsoft's 2024 index says 75% of knowledge workers use AI, and 46% of those users started less than six months earlier. (Microsoft WorkLab, 2024) Using AI is already normal, but having a shared plan is not. Leaders worry about this, since 60% of them say their company lacks a plan and vision. Another 55% of leaders were worried about finding talent. Only 25% of companies were planning to teach people how to use AI. People are already in the tools, and almost nobody is showing them a shared way to work.

Your staff are probably using AI already, with or without a plan. Among AI users, 78% bring their own tools to work, and that number is 80% at small and midsize businesses. At a small firm that often means a personal login the owner likes and a different tab the office manager likes. The work lands in the shared inbox, but the method stays in a browser history. When that person is out, the method is out too. That is not a process, because it is only a habit with a password. If you ban the login without writing down the path, the habit just moves somewhere else.

The place where the hours go should decide which job you write first. People spent 60% of their time in the work apps on email, chat, and meetings, and 40% on making new things. Owners often want to automate the part that feels like making something, and they leave the inbox alone. But the inbox is the job, and so is the chat thread. So is the meeting that ends without a note. Making new things is the smaller share of the day. So we sort the daily mess before we polish a rare piece of writing.

Gartner's January 2026 article says at least 50% of generative AI projects were dropped after the first test run by the end of the year before. It names poor data, weak risk checks, rising costs, and unclear value as the causes. (Gartner, 2026) We don't read that as a reason to fear the tools. We read it as a picture of demos that never had a job attached. Poor data shows up when nobody decided which record is the real one. Weak risk checks show up when nobody owns the stop button. Rising costs show up when the test keeps growing because the goal was never one written path. Unclear value shows up when you can't point at the step that got easier to finish. Then the project is dropped, and the report blames the model. The missing page never makes it into the report.

Write down the steps a person already follows. Mark the step that waits for a judgment, and automate the steps that don't. If every step needs a judgment, you don't have a process yet, you have a craft. A craft can still get help at the edges, such as drafts, reminders, and a place for the file to land. But it should not be sold a machine that pretends to replace the judgment. We would rather say that on the first call. Then nobody pays for a pilot that looks just like the pile Gartner described.

## A worked example

Take a trades desk as the example we walk through. This is not a measured result and it is not a trophy story. It is the shape of the afternoon we keep seeing when we ask someone to tell us about yesterday. The owner prices the work and the office manager answers the phone. A lead tech visits the site and comes back with a note that is half measurements and half memory. The bookkeeper sends the invoice only after someone says the job is done.

Yesterday's quote starts as a voicemail. The office manager jots down the name, the street, the room, and a mention of a leak. The lead tech visits and takes photos on a personal phone. Then he texts a few of them to the owner with a line saying the job isn't bad. The owner opens an old quote, changes a few lines, and sets the price from a similar job they remember. The bookkeeper never sees any of it until the customer says yes. Sometimes the yes arrives as a text to the owner, who means to forward it and forgets.

When we sit there and write the path, it becomes ordinary in the best way. The office manager logs the address and the room before the visit is booked. The lead tech files the measurements and the photos before leaving the driveway. The owner prices the job from that note, and the price is the step that waits for a person. The office manager sends the quote only after the price is on it. The bookkeeper opens the invoice only after the yes is written down. We would not hand the price to a model. The rest is copying, ordering, and waiting for a mark. A simple system can carry the note, remind the tech about a missing measurement, and hold the quote. A person still sends it. What the bookkeeper wants is usually small. It is a written yes, a matching price, and the same spelling of the name on the invoice. That is a handoff.

A clinic has the same shape with different words. The front desk takes the call, and the practitioner decides whether the visit is something they can help with. Billing waits for both. Once those steps are written, the front desk can draft the confirmation while a person still sends it. If nobody writes them, someone buys a tool that claims to handle intake. Meanwhile the practitioner keeps a side pad that becomes the real process. A shop counter looks simpler, which is why owners skip the page. The Saturday clerk and the owner tell two different stories when we ask each of them how a reorder really happens. We write both versions down before anyone opens a settings screen.

## How we'd run it

## Generative Engine Optimization vs SEO

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/generative-engine-optimization-vs-seo

Google says the new names are still SEO. A research paper measures visibility. Pew measured the click. Write the page so both can use it.

In Google's own guide, generative engine optimization and SEO are the same craft. The page still has to be worth reading by a person. The idea that you must pick a side is a sales pitch, and it is not how the guide is written.

Google says answer-engine optimization and generative-engine optimization are still SEO. (Google Search Central) The page has to be in Google's list of pages, and it has to be allowed to show as a snippet. Google does not use llms.txt, and it does not ask you to chop the page up in any special way. We keep those lines together because owners are being told to pay for a second program beside the first one. The guide does not describe a second program. It only describes the page you already owed your reader, which is now being quoted inside an answer.

The [visibility guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/visibility) is how you check whether that page can be found and quoted. The [answer-engine note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/answer-engine-optimization) lists the methods in one place, if you want them. The [llms.txt note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/what-is-llms-txt) covers the file Google says it ignores. That is good to know before someone sells it to you as the gap between the two names.

## What changes, and what does not

The 2024 paper says that pages written for a generated answer gained up to 40% in how often they showed up. (arXiv, 2024) Adding quotes, sources, and facts with numbers went with gains of over 40%. On Perplexity the gains went up to 37%. The study also saw a 41% rise in word count, adjusted for position. It saw a 28% rise in how the reader felt about the answer. All of this came from a set of 10,000 questions. So what changes, in that study, is how easy it is to spot a source inside the answer when the writing carries proof. What does not change is the need for a real page that a robot can read and a person can use.

Keep the two layers apart when a pitch blurs them. SEO, the way Google uses the word, gets the page into its list and ready to be quoted as a snippet. The generative layer is what happens when an answer borrows from that page. You can fail the first layer and never reach the second one. You can also get quoted and still fail the business, if the quote told the reader enough and the visit never came. Both failures belong to the same page, so they are not two departments.

Pew found, in July 2025, that people clicked a link 8% of the time when a search showed an AI summary. When it showed none, they clicked 15% of the time. (Pew Research Center, 2025) SEO still gets the page into the list, and the page still has to be worth the click.

That is the plain split we want owners to remember. Getting into the list is the price of a seat. The click is what pays for the chair time, the staff, and the front desk. A page written only to be summed up will do the first job and skip the second. A page that is only a thin list of keywords will do neither one well. A summary has nothing solid to lift, and a person has nothing solid to trust.

## A worked example

Take a small dental clinic as an example, and not as a case with a score. The front desk lead already answers the same questions that people type into the search box. The dentist will not let the website make up promises about care. The questions the owner cares about are the ones new patients ask before they call. They want to know what happens at a first visit. They ask whether it is okay to bring up a cracked tooth. They also ask whether the clinic will see someone who is nervous.

The page they have today is an SEO page in the old, thin way. It has a city name, the words "family dentistry," a list of services, and a map. It might be in Google's list, but a snippet from it would be mush. Say someone asks an answer engine about a cracked tooth and a nervous patient. It will skip that page for one that says what the first hour is like. That other page tells you what to bring and what the clinic will not promise. The owner does not need a second site for these readers. She only needs this one page to do both jobs.

What does not change is the floor. The page has to be in Google's list and ready to show as a snippet. The front desk lead should be able to read the first lines and say, "Yes, that is what I tell people." The dentist should be able to read the clinical lines without wincing. If those two cannot sign off on the page, no engine should be quoting it. Google's no to special chopping and to llms.txt fits here too. Breaking the page into bits does not help, and neither does adding a side file. Nothing takes the place of the owner standing behind each sentence.

What changes is the shape of the sentences. The paper is why we say so, though we will not turn it into a promise. In that 2024 work, quotes, sources, and facts with numbers went with gains of over 40%, on a set of 10,000 questions. For this clinic, the honest version is small. Quote the after-care steps you already hand out on paper. Name the rules you really follow when you talk about a cracked tooth, and skip the blog that only sounds like a doctor. If you give a number, it should be one you can explain. A patient may read it in an answer and walk in holding it. Word count and the reader score moved in the study, by 41% and 28%. We do not make those a goal for the owner. We turn them into a simple rule, which is to write enough real detail that a reader can feel the visit before they book.

The click problem sits on top of that. Pew is why we will not let the page stop at what a cracked tooth is. A summary can explain the tooth, but the page has to explain this clinic. First visits start with a talk and not a surprise procedure. Nervous patients can say so when they book, and the front desk lead will set aside a longer time in the chair. The clinic does not do every kind of care, and it will say which kinds it sends elsewhere. A summary that only wanted a definition has no use for those lines, and they are the reason a person still taps through. In the July 2025 Pew look, people clicked 8% of the time when a summary showed, against 15% when none did. So write the lines the summary cannot cover.

Now the jobs again, because this is where projects get sloppy. The owner approves what the clinic claims. The front desk lead checks the practical lines against the phone script, including the list of places the clinic sends people. The dentist owns anything that could sound like a diagnosis or a promise of no pain. A freelancer can tidy the headings, but a freelancer cannot decide where the clinic sends people. Say the generative work and the SEO work are billed as two projects. You will get two drafts that disagree, and the patient will find that out at the front desk.

## How we'd run it

We would run one page, one time, for both names.

First, pick the one question the front desk lead answers every week, and write about only that.

## How Can AI Help a Small Business? What Surveys Count

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses

Two 2025 surveys count different work. This note separates generative-AI use from AI in production, then names the jobs owners hand over.

AI helps a small business when it takes over a named job that a person already does. It does not help by moving you closer to a headline. Two surveys from 2025 count AI in small firms, and they count different kinds of work. The U.S. Chamber asked who uses generative AI. Statistics Canada asked who used AI to make goods or to deliver services. A firm can say yes to the first and no to the second, and both answers can be honest. This note keeps those two claims apart, and then it names the jobs that owners hand over. The [pressure guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/pressure) asks the matching question for one business, and we write these notes on [our site](/).

We sit with owners who have already been told they are late. The number they heard was usually the bigger one. So the first thing we do is find out what that number really measures. Help, for a shop or a clinic or a trades desk, looks like a draft that someone checks. It looks like a sort that someone trusts, or a reminder that someone still sends. It is not a rank on a national chart.

## Generative use is not production use

The Chamber's small business report says 58% of small businesses called themselves users of generative AI. (U.S. Chamber of Commerce) That is up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023. That question is about generative AI. It does not ask whether AI makes the goods or the service. The owner said so, and no one watched the work to check. It also does not mean the tool is part of the product. An owner who drafts a customer email and then rewrites half of it can answer yes. We would answer yes with them. That yes is real, but it is a different fact from a system that makes the thing the customer bought.

Statistics Canada ran its Canadian Survey on Business Conditions for the second quarter of 2025. It found that 12.2% of businesses used AI to make goods or deliver services. (Statistics Canada, 2025) That is up from 6.1% in the second quarter of 2024. The release is dated 16 June 2025, and the survey ran from 1 April to 5 May 2025. The agency got 21,357 responses, and 9,103 of them came from businesses that used AI. Read those counts as a picture of who was asked, and not as a target. A big response still describes the questions that were asked. It does not turn the generative question into the production question.

Among the businesses that used AI, 35.7% used text analytics and 23.1% used marketing automation. Then 40.1% had made new workflows, and 38.9% had trained their staff. Those shares sit inside the group that already uses AI. They are not shares of every firm in the country, and they are not shares of the Chamber's question. Text analytics means reading and sorting words. Marketing automation means sending messages and counting what comes back. A new workflow is a path that was not written down before. Training means a person was shown that path. Put that way, the list is practical, and it is also modest. None of the four says the business now runs itself.

## Jobs an owner can hand over

The Chamber number describes a tool that someone opens. The StatCan number describes AI inside the making of the product or the service. A small business can do the first for a long time without ever doing the second. We think that is a sane order. Open the tool on a job you can check. Ask the production question later, when the goods or the service truly depend on the system. Most owners we sit with are nowhere near that later question, and they do not need to pretend they are.

The jobs in the StatCan list are the practical ones. They are reading and sorting text and sending and measuring marketing. They are also writing a workflow that did not exist and training the people who will run it. None of them is a promise that the tool will run the business. Reading text looks like an inbox, a pile of referrals or a supplier sheet. Sending marketing looks like a note to people who already bought from you. It is not a brand campaign with a film crew. A new workflow looks like a page the front desk can follow. The owner can be in a room with a patient at the time. Training looks like sitting with that person once on a real message. It does not look like a slide deck made for a big company.

The [readiness note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) asks a different question. It asks whether this firm has the data, the process, the people and the decision in place. It does not ask about the average firm. Average firms are what surveys are for, but your firm is a counter, a desk and a schedule. If the readiness questions fail, the survey numbers will not save the project. If they pass, you still do not need the bigger number as a goal. What you need is the job.

## A worked example

Take a clinic as the walkthrough. The owner saw the Chamber number and felt late, because friends in a group chat were already using it. The front desk still types appointment reminders by hand. The practitioner still scribbles the note after each visit, and billing still waits for someone to say the visit happened. Nothing in that room makes care through a model. The care is the practitioner. The model may come in at all. If it does, it comes in as a draft of a reminder. Or it comes in as a cleaner version of a note that the practitioner will still sign.

Walk the reminder first, because it happens every day and a wrong one is easy to spot. The front desk has the visit in the book. A draft can say the time, the place and what to bring. The front desk reads it, because some patients need a phone call and some need a short message. The draft does not know the difference. The practitioner is not in that choice unless the reminder holds a clinical instruction, and then the practitioner reads it. Billing does not need to see it at all. That is three roles and one job, and we named the handoff.

A shop down the street is even plainer, which is why the headline feels insulting there. The owner sorts supplier mail and customer questions in the same inbox. Sorting is text work, so a system can group the supplier sheets away from the sizing questions. The owner still decides which question gets an answer before lunch. The goods on the shelf were not made by a model. If the shop says it uses AI because the inbox got grouped, that is the Chamber kind of yes. If it said it uses AI to make the goods, that would be the StatCan question. The honest answer would be no.

A trades desk sits between the two. The lead tech's site note is text, and turning it into a description the customer can read is a draft. The owner still sets the price, and the service is still the repair. You are near the production question only when the job truly depends on the system. A friend forwarding a chart does not count. Until then, hand over the draft and keep the price.

## How we'd run it

First, write down which survey sentence you heard. If it was about generative use, say so in a full sentence.

… Full post: https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses
