2. Analysis in Brief, artificial intelligence use by businesses in Canada — Statistics Canada, 2025-06-16 — https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/11-621-m/11-621-m2025008-eng.htm

## How Client Work Moves Through HQ and Our AI Agents

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/how-client-work-flows-through-hq

A request comes in, HQ files it, Grok Bot agents build it, Client Services checks it, and our team signs off before it lands in your own HQ space.

Here is the short answer. A client sends us a request, and HQ turns it into a card on that client's board. Grok Bot agents with the right skills build the work and file it back to HQ, where it is held. Client Services checks it against the request, and a person on our team approves it. Only then does it appear in the client's own space in HQ.

This note walks through each step. HQ also has its own page: see [HQ, the client workspace](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/products/hq/). The path below is the same one we use for our own site, and it is the kind of system we build for clients who want agents doing real work. If you are thinking about that, the [AI Readiness Check](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check) is the place to start. It gives you next steps for your business.

## What happens when you send us a request?

Most requests start as an email to magic@abra-ca-dabra.app. HQ logs each message that reaches that inbox and puts it in front of Client Services. Routine questions get a quick reply from our Client Services assistant, and anything that needs a decision goes to a person on our team. If the sender is already a client, the email lands on that client's record. If not, it opens a lead, and we follow up like any new inquiry.

You can also start from the [start a project](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/start/) form on our site. And if you already have work with us, you can ask for changes on a piece right inside your space. All three paths end up in the same place, which is a person or an agent reading what you asked for.

## How does a request become a card in HQ?

Client Services reads the request and hands it to the lead agent for that client. Each client has a lead agent, and some clients have helper agents too. The lead creates a card on the client's board, inside the right project. When Client Services gives it a link to your email, the card keeps that link, so the work always points back to what you asked for.

The board has four columns. They are To do, Doing, Waiting on Client Services, and Done. A new card starts in To do. When an agent picks it up, it moves to Doing. Every move shows up on the client's timeline and in the Client Services feed, so nothing changes without a trace.

## Who builds the work?

The agents do. Each one is a Grok Bot agent that we set up for a client and give a clear role. The lead can keep a card or hand it to a helper agent on the same client. A card can also carry skill packs from our skill library, such as copywriting or search work. The agent reads those skills while it works and can list the ones it followed when it files.

For this note, that meant writing the article, making the pictures and drawing the diagrams. It also meant building the page on the site and testing it before anyone saw it. Agents are fast, but speed is not the point. The point is that a clear request plus the right skills gives a first draft that is worth a careful review.

When an agent is done, it files the work to HQ. A filing carries the files, a short note for our team, and a plain summary written for the client. Filing moves the card to Waiting on Client Services. The files are stored, but they are held, and the client cannot see them yet.

## How does Client Services review it?

Client Services checks the work against the request. Did it answer what was asked? Is anything wrong, missing, or off brand? Are the facts right? If something is off, Client Services sends the card back with a note. The work stays held, and the agent fixes it and files again on the same card.

## Why does a person on our team approve every piece?

Agents can draft a lot of work, and we want all of it checked before it goes out. So nothing is released to a client, and no update is sent, until a person on our team says yes. HQ is built to hold the work until that review is done. By default it does not email clients when work is approved. It drafts an update for us to send ourselves.

Google says it rewards helpful, original content no matter how it was made, and that using AI just to game rankings breaks its rules. (Google Search Central, 2023) We read that as a reason to put a careful review between the draft and the client. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary guide to building trust into how AI is designed, built and used. (NIST, 2023) Ours is a small version of the same idea. A person stays on the hook for what ships.

## What do you see in your HQ space, and when?

While work is held, it stays out of your folders. You won't find it in previews, downloads, shared links or search inside your space, and you get no email about it. Once our team approves it, the files appear in a named folder, like Blog or Social. Each file shows its type, and images get a small thumbnail, so you can tell what is what without opening everything.

The note at the top of each delivery is written for you. It says what we made and what you should look at. It leaves out our internal notes, file paths and agent names.

## What if you want changes?

Ask for them on the piece in your space. HQ opens a new card called Changes requested, with your note on it, in To do. It goes back to the agent that made the work, or to the lead if that agent has moved on. From there it follows the same path again. The agent builds, Client Services checks, and our team approves before you see it.

## Could this work in your business?

This setup is not only for agencies. Any team that gets requests, does work, and sends it back for sign-off can run a version of it. It might be a quote, a report, a page on your site, or a reply to a customer. We build these systems around how your work already flows. Some of them are [custom apps](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/services/custom-apps/), and some are [AI assistants and agents](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/services/ai-assistants-and-agents/). You can see more of what we have shipped in our [portfolio](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/portfolio/). If you want to see HQ itself, including how approved work reaches a social calendar, read the [HQ product page](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/products/hq/). And if agents are new to you, [What Is an AI Agent? A Plain Answer for Owners](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent) is a good place to start.

The first step is knowing where you stand. The [AI Readiness Check](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check) asks how your business runs today. It gives you next steps for your business, with tips for each section. Take it, then [start a project](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/start/) or write to houdini@abra-ca-dabra.app, and we will look at it with you.

2. AI Risk Management Framework — NIST, 2023-01-26 — https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework

## How to Show Up in ChatGPT and AI Overviews

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/how-to-get-your-business-to-show-up-in-chatgpt

Showing up in ChatGPT search is a crawler and indexing problem. Google still treats answer-engine advice as ordinary SEO. Clicks fall when a summary appears.

Getting a business into ChatGPT search starts with the right crawler. That is not the same one OpenAI uses for training, so a mix-up here can undo all the other work. If we block the wrong one, or block all of them, the writing never gets a chance to matter.

OpenAI says it runs separate crawlers. (OpenAI) OAI-SearchBot fetches pages for search results. If you turn it off, your pages stay out of ChatGPT search answers. GPTBot is the crawler for training. ChatGPT-User fetches a page when a person asks for a look-up, and robots.txt may not apply to that one. These are three different jobs, and we repeat that until the owner can say it back to us. Most robots files treat every bot as the same thing. So a rule written in a hurry mixes them up. The mix-up is quiet, because the page just never shows up and someone blames the writing.

The [visibility guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/visibility) reads the site the way a practical check should. It starts with whether a crawler can see the pages at all. The [answer-engine note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/answer-engine-optimization) and the [generative-engine note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/generative-engine-optimization-vs-seo) cover the names people use for Google's summaries. This note stays on the switches, and on the page those switches are meant to show.

## What Google says to do

Google's guide for its generative features says the work is still SEO. (Google Search Central) It says answer-engine work and generative-engine work are both SEO from where Google sits. It says Google does not use llms.txt. It also says there is no special rule for how to chunk a page. The page has to be indexed, and it has to be able to show up as a snippet. No extra schema is needed for these features either. If you came here only for ChatGPT, please do not skip this part, because many owners want both. The Google half of the job is still an ordinary page. A special file will not stand in for it on either side.

Say a page is blocked, thin, or not allowed to show a snippet. It will not turn into an overview because someone added a new file. So we let the search crawler in and keep the page open to indexing. Then we write the answer where a person can read it too.

We see this go wrong in a pattern. First, an agency blocks every bot "for safety," including the search crawler. The owner hears that the site is now protected. Then someone adds a new file because a thread said that file is how you show up. The page underneath is still a list of cities and a phone number. Nothing in that story gives a homeowner an answer they can use. The crawler has to be allowed to fetch. The page has to be open to indexing, and the sentences have to be worth repeating. The file is not the sentence.

Pew found, in July 2025, that visits with an AI summary led to a click 8% of the time. When no summary showed, it was 15%. (Pew Research Center, 2025) That means showing up is not the same as being clicked. So we write the page so that the citation is worth the click.

The Pew study is about Google's summaries, but the habit is the same, so we bring it in here. A generated answer can cover the easy part of a question and leave you unvisited. If you win the mention and lose the call, you have only done half of the job. The page has to carry the part a summary cannot finish. That means who sends the truck, what you will not touch, and how a person books.

## A worked example

Picture an electrical contractor with us. This is a made-up scene, and it is not a measured result. An office manager runs the office, the inbox, and the site password, and two techs do the work. Homeowners ask whether someone can look at a panel that keeps tripping. They also want to know if that person is licensed and insured. And they want someone honest enough to say when the problem is on the utility side.

Their site today is a header, three service words, and a contact form that sometimes fails on a phone. The office manager once pasted a robots file from a forum. A post there said AI companies were copying the web. He did not know he had turned away the crawler that fetches pages for search. Then the owner paid for a rewrite. It added a file at the root and left the service page as thin as before. They were told it would help them show up, but it did not. The search crawler was still shut out, and the page still had nothing a citation could honestly repeat.

So we would split the switches the way OpenAI splits them. OAI-SearchBot has to be allowed if ChatGPT search is going to fetch the panel page. Blocking it keeps the page out of those answers. That is a fair choice if the owner does not want to be there, and a mistake if she does. GPTBot is the training crawler, and that is a separate decision. The owner can say no to training and still want search. She cannot say that with one "disallow all" line she does not understand. ChatGPT-User is the third case, because it fetches when a person asks and robots.txt may not apply. The office manager should know that rule exists. Then he will not tell the owner that a robots file controls every look-up a user can start.

The page itself has to work for a person standing in a dark kitchen. The opening lines answer the panel question. Then they say what you do on a trip and what you will not do. That includes anything on the utility side of the meter. They also say how to reach the office manager. And they say what to tell her so the right tech brings the right tester. The techs should know the description when they read it. They are the ones who will hear "but your website said" in a hallway. The owner signs off on the claims about license and insurance. The office manager signs off on the crawler rules, in writing. The three bots are named in words he can point at.

A generated answer might then mention the firm for a tripping panel in their towns. That mention is not a booking, and Pew is the reminder, even though it measured a different summary. When a summary is on the screen, a click is less common. So the paragraph that the answer cannot replace is the one about the utility line. It also covers calling the office manager with a photo of the panel label. The citation makes them curious, and the clear refusal gets them to the phone. A thin page only gets them a sentence that could have been about any electrician in the county.

## How we'd run it

We would fix the robots file and the service page in the same week. We would not call a new root file the project.

First, write the three crawlers in the office manager's notebook in plain words. OAI-SearchBot fetches pages for search, and leaving it blocked keeps you out of ChatGPT search answers. GPTBot is for training. ChatGPT-User fetches when a person asks for a look-up, and a robots file may not control it. If the office manager cannot tell them apart yet, nobody edits the file.

Second, decide the training question on purpose.

## How to Use AI in Your Business: Twelve Jobs

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/how-to-use-ai-in-your-business

Pick a job you already do, write the steps, and keep a person on the output. A Canadian survey shows which uses, and which follow-on work, are common.

Using AI in a business starts with a list of jobs, not a list of tools. Pick a job you already do and write down the steps. Then keep a person on the result. The tool is the last thing you choose, and for many jobs it is a small one.

Statistics Canada asked businesses that already use AI which tools they use and what they changed. (Statistics Canada, 2025) In its 2025 report, 35.7% of them used text analytics, which is software that reads and sorts written text. Another 23.1% used marketing automation. Also, 40.1% had built new ways of working, and 38.9% had trained their staff. In the same report, 12.2% of all businesses used AI to make goods or give a service, up from 6.1% a year before. These numbers show what firms said they did. They are not a shopping list, so there is no reason to open twelve tools on Monday.

The [help note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/how-can-ai-help-small-businesses) explains the gap between making goods with AI and using AI to write and sort. The [automation note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-automation-for-small-business) shows how to pick the first job. The [agents note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-agents-for-business) covers the time when the steps start to branch, and a fixed checklist no longer fits. We'd start with one job from the list below. Then we'd leave the rest alone until that job has a person on it and a week of real use behind it.

## Twelve jobs you can write down

In each job below, AI does the first try and a person makes the call.

- AI drafts the customer reply, and a person sends it.
- AI sums up the meeting, and a person accepts the tasks.
- AI turns notes into a quote, and a person sets the price.
- AI sorts the inbox, and a person decides what gets an answer.
- AI flags the late bill, and a person decides how to chase it.
- AI describes the product, and a person approves the page.
- AI groups the help requests, and a person picks the answer.
- AI spots the stock problem, and a person places the order.
- AI rewrites the policy in plain words, and a person posts it.
- AI compares two supplier notes, and a person chooses.
- AI drafts the weekly report, and a person accepts the numbers.
- AI prepares the staff answer, and a person trains the staff.

Every line has the same shape. The tool gets the work ready, and a person decides. If you take the person out, you no longer have a job. You have a mailbox that hopes for the best. The reply can be drafted from the thread the customer wrote, but someone who knows that customer still sends it. The meeting summary can list the tasks, but someone who was in the room still accepts them. The tool was not there to hear the aside that mattered. The quote can be built from notes, but the price stays with the owner. We keep coming back to this shape because owners try to skip the second half, and the second half is the business.

The numbers above are about businesses that already use AI, except the 12.2% figure. That one covers all businesses in the Canadian survey. So please don't read the text analytics share as a share of every firm. When we say 35.7%, we mean that share of the businesses already using AI, not the shop on the corner. Marketing automation at 23.1% is the same kind of share. The 40.1% and 38.9% for new ways of working and training are also among firms that already use AI. They tell you what those firms changed. They don't say that a firm that has never tried this is behind, and they don't say which of the twelve jobs to run first. The 12.2% figure stands apart, and we don't want it mixed in with the others. Using a tool to draft a reply is a different claim from using AI to make the goods or give the service.

## A worked example

Take a shop we keep using as our walkthrough. It is not a case study or a scoreboard. It is just a counter, a back room, and three people. The owner buys and sets prices, a clerk covers the floor and the inbox, and a bookkeeper chases what was not paid.

Yesterday, in this story, looked like any other day. A customer emailed about a size, and a supplier sent a new price sheet. Two bills sat past the date the bookkeeper cares about. A talk with the landlord left a page of scribbles and no tasks. The product page for a new item was still blank. None of that needs a new company, but someone does need to say which of those is the job for now.

Say they pick the customer reply, because it comes up every day. A wrong tone with a regular costs more than any chart can show. The clerk drops the thread into a draft. The draft pulls in the size the customer asked about and the line the owner uses for delays. The clerk reads it and changes one sentence, because this customer dislikes cheery notes. Then the clerk sends it. The tool did not know about the cheery notes, but the clerk did, and that is the whole design.

You can sort the inbox in the same pass if you like. A person still decides what gets answered today and what can wait. The late bill goes on a list the bookkeeper already trusts, and the bookkeeper decides how to chase it. A stiff note to a good account takes good sense. A reminder to a stranger who has been quiet for sixty days is closer to a rule. Even then, we like a person to take a quick look.

The quote job shows up the day the shop does custom work. Notes from a talk become a description, and the owner sets the price. We've watched owners let the draft set the price because it sounded sure of itself. But sounding sure is not the same as knowing the cost. The supplier comparison is the same trap in a different coat. There are two notes with two minimums and two lead times, all written in different ways. A draft can line them up. The owner chooses, because choosing is the job and lining up is only the chore.

A clinic can run the same list without acting like a shop. The practitioner accepts the tasks from the meeting summary, and a person trains the staff on the answer the tool prepared. A person also posts the plain-word policy. That step matters because a policy that sounds friendly but says the wrong thing about care is worse than a stiff one that is right. A trades desk lives in the quote and the stock problem. The lead tech's note becomes a description, and the owner sets the price. Then a person checks the problem and places the order. We are not saying every firm should run all twelve. We are saying that each of the twelve is a job with an edge, and the edge is a person.

## How we'd run it

First, write the twelve down where the owner can see them, in the firm's own words. "Flag the late bill" might mean "the Tuesday list the bookkeeper already prints." So use that name for it. A job you can't say in their words is not a job you can hand over.

Second, pick one with a simple test. It should happen often, the result should be easy to check, and a mistake should show up before a customer gets hurt. The customer reply and the late bill flag usually pass that test.

… Full post: https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/how-to-use-ai-in-your-business

Sources
1. Analysis in Brief, artificial intelligence use by businesses in Canada — Statistics Canada, 2025-06-16 — https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/11-621-m/11-621-m2025008-eng.htm

## Is My Business Ready for AI? Signs to Read First

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/is-my-business-ready-for-ai

Ready means the data, the process, the people, and the decision can carry a tool. This note reads those signs against a large-firm index.

A business is ready for AI when one named job can move to a tool without anyone inventing the process along the way. Ready is not a mood, and it is not a purchase. It describes the data, the process, the people, and the decision around that one job. If any one of those four is still a shrug, then the job is not ready yet.

The [Readiness Check](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check) asks about these same signs. (Abracadabra AI) It gives you next steps for your business. Each sentence on the check describes a state of the business. The check does not diagnose anything, and we like that limit. A diagnosis invites shame, but a state invites the next piece of work. Not ready yet is allowed to be the true state. Plenty of good businesses are not ready on the job they just tried to automate, and they are fine at the rest of their work.

The [readiness guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/readiness) spells out those states in full sentences. The [assessment note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-readiness-assessment) compares the public tools side by side. Read the guide when you want the exact wording. Read this note when you want to know which signs to trust before a vendor tells you what the signs are.

## What a large-firm index is counting

Cisco's 2025 AI Readiness Index surveyed 8,000 senior leaders at organizations with more than 500 employees, across 30 markets and 26 industries. (Cisco, 2025) The firms it called pacesetters were near 13% of that sample, and they were 4 times more likely to move a pilot into production. That sample is not a census of small businesses. So a small firm can be ready for one job and still look nothing like a pacesetter.

We say that last part slowly, because owners often miss it. Ready, in this note, means the named job can carry a tool. A pacesetter in Cisco's index is a large organization in a sample of senior leaders, and the 13% describes those organizations. It is not a report card for a shop, a clinic, or a trades desk. Suppose a salesperson says you should buy now to catch up with the pacesetters. Then they have glued a large-firm statistic to a small-firm fear. The 4 times gap in moving pilots into production is real inside that sample. It does not mean your service writer is late.

Use the index as a picture of a different size of firm. The useful part is that moving a pilot into production follows a written process. The useless move is to decide you are behind a business that staffs a whole crew for its pilot. You have a bay, a desk, and a person who knows the customers. Readiness is whether that person can hand the job to a tool without the job falling apart.

The OECD SME AI adoption tool is part of 2026 Group of Seven work. It is a short self-check for smaller firms. (OECD) It takes about five minutes, keeps the answers in the browser, and does not publish an adoption rate. We'd use it as a second set of questions and not as a national share. A second set helps because our own questions can go stale in our own mouths. Someone else's short check, with no stored data and no pretend rate, is a good way to see whether you dodged a theme. It will not tell you whether small firms in your country are ready. If someone finishes it and announces a countrywide rate, they have added a sentence the tool refused to say.

We look for four signs that a job can move to a tool. The one place the facts live has a name, the steps are written down, a person owns the output, and someone can stop the experiment. We also look for four signs that it cannot move. The knowledge sits in one head, the exceptions are unwritten, nobody may send the output to a customer, and success has no definition.

The signs are easy to see when the person who does the job is in the room. "Named" means you can point at one record, and the other records lose the argument. "Written" means a new person could follow the exceptions and not only the sunny path. "Owns the output" means a human is accountable for what a customer receives. "Can stop" means someone may halt a bad send without asking the vendor.

The bad signs are the same facts turned around. Knowledge in one head feels like loyalty to a great employee, but it also means the job stops when that person is out. Unwritten exceptions feel like flexibility, but they are where a tool will start to improvise. Nobody being allowed to send feels like caution, until you notice that someone is already sending from a personal account. And success with no definition is how a pilot turns into a subscription.

A small firm can show the good signs on one job and the bad signs on another. That is normal, and it is why "is my business ready?" is the wrong question. The honest question is which job. The signs describe the state you are in, based on how you answered, and they are not a tattoo on the business. Not ready yet is a description, and so is ready. Neither one means you have bought a product, and neither one means you have failed as an owner.

## A worked example

Say we are in an independent auto shop on a slow afternoon. One person writes the service tickets, and another is the lead tech. This is an example we walk through, so we are not reporting their revenue, how often cars come back, or any other number. We did not measure those, and we will not fake them.

The owner asked after a vendor showed a tool that drafts customer updates from the ticket. We split the question and asked which job she meant. The job on offer is the status text. The lead tech finds what is wrong, the customer hears it and says yes or no, and then the lead tech goes ahead or does not.

Walk the good signs. Is there one place the facts live, and does it have a name? The ticket writer says it is the shop system. The lead tech says she writes the real finding on the paper that stays on the dash. The system ticket holds only what the ticket writer had time to type, and he is often still with the last customer. The owner says she trusts whatever the ticket writer texts her. That makes three candidates, so the source is not named, and that is the first bad sign already. The true finding sits on the lead tech's paper and in her head, which is the "one head" sign, even though the ticket writer has a system. A system that nobody believes is not the one place the facts live.

Are the steps written down? The sunny path is written, and it goes car in, inspect, call, approve, repair, car out. The exceptions are not written. What if the customer does not answer and the bay is needed? What if the lead tech finds a second problem after the yes? What if the ticket writer is off and the other writer does not know the lead tech's shorthand? Those are unwritten exceptions, and that is the second bad sign.

Does a person own the output? The vendor's tool would send a text, and the ticket writer assumes he would glance at it. The lead tech says she would not see it until the customer called angry.

… Full post: https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/is-my-business-ready-for-ai

2. Cisco AI research: the most AI-ready companies — Cisco, 2025-10-14 — https://newsroom.cisco.com/c/r/newsroom/en/us/a/y2025/m10/cisco-ai-research-the-most-ai-ready-companies-outpace-peers-in-the-race-to-value.html
3. OECD SME AI adoption tool — OECD — https://sme.oecd.ai/

## Off-the-Shelf AI or Custom Software

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/off-the-shelf-ai-or-custom-software

Buy the product when it already does the job. Build only when the job is yours alone. Surveys show generative AI use is already common among small firms.

Off-the-shelf AI is the right buy when a product already does the job. Custom software is the right build when the job is special to how your business works and no product covers it. We start there because owners usually start at the other end. They hear that serious firms build, or they hear that nobody should build. Both speeches skip the one question that matters. Does a product already do this job, with a person you can name checking the output? If yes, buy it. If the job depends on your records, your exceptions, and your checker, a product will not make those up for you. That is the custom case, and it is rarer than the sales talk suggests.

The [studio](/) takes the work that products do not cover. The [consultant note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-consultant-for-small-business) covers what to ask before you pick either path. The [agency comparison](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-automation-agency-vs-consultant) covers who to hire once you know you are building. It also helps if you know you should not be. We would rather lose a build than make a custom frame for a job that a sealed box already does. The box is not an insult. The box is how a small firm stays small instead of becoming a software company by accident.

## What the surveys count

The Chamber's 2025 report says 58% of small businesses use generative AI, up from 40% in 2024 and 23% in 2023. (U.S. Chamber of Commerce) That is a claim about use. It is not a claim that those firms built their own software. Use can mean a tab someone opened, or a draft written inside a product they already pay for. The rise over those years says owners are trying the tools. It does not say they hired anyone to build something new. When a pitch borrows the 58% and then offers you a custom build, it has quietly changed the subject. The subject was use, but the bill is for a build, and those are two different purchases.

Salesforce asked 3,350 leaders at firms with 200 employees or fewer. (Salesforce, 2024) In that survey, 75% were at least trying out AI, and 83% of growing small and midsize businesses said the same. Among firms already using AI, 91% said it boosts revenue. The survey does not say whether those tools were bought or built. Read that last sentence twice before you let a revenue line pick your plan. "At least trying out" is a very wide door. A revenue boost among people already using AI does not name a vendor. It does not name a pile of code you will have to feed, either. We have heard that revenue line used as a reason to build, but the line has no idea what was bought.

If a bought product covers the job, buy it. If the job depends on your records, your exceptions, and your checker, the product will not make those up, and that is the custom case. Records means the files you really keep, not the files a demo pretended you had. Exceptions means the customer you treat differently and the job you turn down. The checker means a named person who can say the output is wrong. If you miss any one of the three, you do not have a custom case. You have a wish that someone will design your business while they design the software.

## A worked example

Take a shop whose reorder list already lives in the register. This is a walkthrough, not a result. The owner gets a flag when a staple item runs low, and the Saturday clerk trusts that flag enough to pull a box. The bookkeeper does not need a second opinion unless the flag is about a special order. A cousin in another trade told the owner to "build something with AI" after seeing a demo. Building here would mean a second list that drifts away from the register. It would also mean a login the clerk will not open on a busy Saturday. And the new list still could not tell a staple from a special order any better than the flag can. So keep the product you have, and spend your time on the one exception the flag gets wrong. Write down who decides that exception, and you are done. It might be a setting, or it might be a sentence on the wall, but it is not a custom build.

A trades desk is where we stop saying buy so quickly. A quote starts as a voicemail. Then it becomes a site note, picks up photos from the lead tech's phone, and waits for the owner to set a price. The office manager sends it only after the price is there. No product they already pay for holds that whole stack. The accounting tool holds the invoice after the customer says yes, and the inbox holds the mess before that. A bought AI assistant can draft a friendly note and still lose the measurement. Custom, in this room, means a path that keeps the measurement, the photo, and the price gap together until the owner fills the gap. The price stays a gap on purpose, because we will not build a system that makes up a price. If a vendor says their shelf product already does the whole path, make them run yesterday's quote in front of you. If they can, buy it. If they redraw your job until it fits their screens, you are back in the custom case. Or you are in the case where you change your job to fit a product. Changing the job is allowed. Pretending you did not change it is how the build gets blamed later.

A clinic usually looks like the shop until someone describes intake. Plain reminders are a product, and many booking tools already send them. Do not order a reminder engine just so the waiting room can say you built something. The custom candidate is the odd part of intake. That might be the practitioner's rules about which visits are in scope, or the note that billing needs. It might be the patient who must be called instead of messaged. If those rules live only in the practitioner's head, a product will not make them up. A custom build would only lock in a bad guess. Write the rules down first, and then see whether a product has a place to put them. Only the leftover is a build. We have watched clinics jump to the leftover and then find that the booking tool had a field for it all along. The field is not glamorous, and glamour is a poor reason to hire a developer.

## How we'd run it

First, write the job as one sentence with a person on the output. The clerk acts on the reorder flag. The owner sets the price after the note is complete. The front desk sends the reminder after reading it. If the sentence has no person in it, you do not yet know what you are buying or building. You are really just shopping for a good feeling.

Second, list the products you already pay for and ask, in writing, whether any of them do that sentence. Ask the person who uses the product, not only the person who gets the bill. The bookkeeper knows whether late invoices are already flagged. The clerk knows whether the reorder flag tells the truth. The front desk knows whether reminders already go out. A consultant helps here when the owner is too close to the demo to see the product they already have.

Third, try the shelf product on yesterday's real job before you talk to a builder. Do not use a sample record.

… Full post: https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/off-the-shelf-ai-or-custom-software

Sources
1. Empowering Small Business Report 2025 — U.S. Chamber of Commerce — https://www.uschamber.com/assets/documents/Empowering-Small-Business-Report-2025.pdf
2. New research reveals SMBs with AI adoption see stronger revenue growth — Salesforce, 2024-12-04 — https://www.salesforce.com/news/stories/smbs-ai-trends-2025/

## What Is an AI Agent? A Plain Answer for Owners

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/what-is-an-ai-agent

An agent chooses a step from what it just found. A workflow follows a path you wrote. This note uses Anthropic's split and McKinsey's count of who is scaling.

An AI agent is a computer program that looks at what it just found and then picks its own next step. It stays inside limits that you set. A workflow is different, because it does the steps in an order that someone wrote down ahead of time. We use that split whenever an owner asks us if the new line on the invoice is a real agent or just a form with a louder name.

Anthropic's December 2024 essay draws the line the same way. In a workflow, large language models (the kind of AI that reads and writes text) follow a path that the builder set up. In an agent, the model directs its own process and decides which tools to use. (Anthropic, 2024) The essay also says to start with the simplest thing that works. Add more only when the simple version fails. We keep that advice on the table during these talks.

Most of the businesses we sit with are not stuck because their software is too plain. They are stuck because the work still lives in one person's memory. Then a seller asks a model to make up a process that nobody ever wrote down.

If the steps are still in someone's head, the [process guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-process-low) is the check that fits. The [use-case note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-agents-for-business) lists jobs that a system might take over. The [comparison note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-agents-vs-agentic-ai) stays on the words, which is where sales pages get slippery.

## When a workflow is enough

Use a workflow when you already know the steps. Think of taking an email, pulling out the details, writing a draft, and waiting for a person to look at it. Use an agent when the next step depends on what the last step found, and you cannot write down every branch ahead of time. If you cannot say when the system should stop, you do not really have either one yet.

Picture a plumbing desk on a loud Monday. The scheduler runs the book, so she gets the name, the address, and whether there is water on the floor. Then she asks which room it is in and whether anyone shut off the main. Those questions do not change just because a model showed up. A workflow can hold them in a form, a text to the on-call tech, and a line in the book. The fork comes after that intake, and it is the part people like to skip.

A restaurant with water coming through the ceiling is a very different promise from a slow drip under a rental sink. The restaurant needs the owner or the senior tech to say if someone rolls right now. The drip can wait for the afternoon route. Sellers offer an agent for that fork, one that reads the note and picks a tech, a part, and a time. We would let it draft the options. We would not let it text a time until the scheduler or the owner has looked. If the order is known, a workflow will do. If the order depends on what you just learned, an agent may help, and you still want a person who can stop the send.

Here is how the three kinds of system compare. With one prompt, the person at the keyboard picks the next step, and it fits a single draft or a single answer. With a workflow, the path you wrote picks the next step, and it fits work where the steps rarely change. With an agent, the model picks the next step inside the limits you set, and it fits work where the path depends on what it finds.

Read that before you read any product page. With one prompt, the person is still choosing. They paste in the job notes, ask for a reply, and send it themselves, which can save a tired afternoon. That is not an agent, and it does not need to become one. A workflow means you know the order, and the software repeats it without getting bored or skipping the address. An agent means the model looks at what it found and picks a tool, such as the calendar, the parts list, or the text message. The limits are yours, because you decide which tools exist, what the system may never send, and who holds the stop.

That last test is the one we use with owners. If the steps rarely change, stop shopping and write down the path. If the path depends on what the system finds, you may want an agent. You still want the limits on one page that a new hire could follow. We have watched shops pay for an agent to do work that belongs in a simple workflow. Then the staff spends the week fixing a machine that was never supposed to decide anything.

## What the survey actually counts

Owners hear a loud number and think the whole trade has already moved past them. McKinsey's 2025 survey says that 88% of people report regular AI use in at least one part of their business, up from 78% a year earlier. (McKinsey) That is a wide claim, because regular use can mean a person pasting a quote into a chat window on a Thursday. It is a very different thing from saying "we run an agent."

The numbers about agents are smaller, and they are the ones we want in the room. About 23% say their companies are rolling out an AI agent system somewhere, and another 39% are trying agents out. In any single part of the business, no more than 10% say they are rolling out agents. Read that last number slowly. An agent somewhere in a big company is not the same as an agent running the scheduling desk. Companies that earn less than $100 million a year are less often at the wide rollout stage, at 29%. Nearly half of the companies that earn more than $5 billion are further along.

Those are survey shares for big groups of companies. They are not a score for one small business. An agent still needs a written process and a person who can stop it.

We say this out loud because the big percentage gets used as a shove. A seller will put the 88% on a slide and talk as if a shop with a few trucks is running late. The survey does not say that. It says use is common, and rolling out an agent inside one team is not. If companies with real operations teams are mostly still trying things, you are allowed to write down your process first. You can do that before you buy a system that picks its own tools. The survey is a count of what people said. It is not a definition of an agent, and it is not a grade for your desk.

## A worked example

Stay with the plumbing desk and give everyone a job. This is a walk-through and not a result we measured. The owner takes the hard calls, a scheduler runs the book, and Luis and Priya work on the trucks.

A property manager calls about a smell in more than one unit. The scheduler opens the job the way she always does. She takes the name, a callback number, the address, the keys, and whether anyone is home. That part is a workflow, and it should not depend on a model's mood. Then the notes get messy. One unit had a dishwasher replaced not long ago, and another has a tenant who shuts off the water and tells nobody. A third unit is empty. The next step depends on what the scheduler just heard. Which door gets the first visit? Should the truck carry a camera? Is a smell in an empty unit a bigger problem than a clogged trap?

## What Is llms.txt, and Who Actually Reads It

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/what-is-llms-txt

A proposed file that points models at your best pages. Google says it does not use the file. A large study found most copies are never requested.

llms.txt is a text file that someone proposed putting at the top level of a website. It lists the pages you most want an AI model to read, so think of it as a map. It is not a citation, and it does not change how you rank.

Jeremy Howard published the proposal in September 2024, and the page was updated in August 2026. (llmstxt.org, 2024) The idea is a short list of pages for a model to read. It should be written so that a person can check it in one sitting. This site already has [its own file](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/llms.txt), and that is a fact about this site, not a traffic number. We publish it because we like having a clean list of what we stand behind.

Google's guide says that Google does not use llms.txt for its AI features in search. (Google Search Central) We keep that next to the proposal, or the proposal turns into a rumor. A file that Google's AI features do not read cannot be the reason you show up in them. The page still has to be indexed, and it still has to deserve the quote.

To find out whether your file is missing, broken, or pointing at junk, use the [missing-file guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/missing-llms-txt) is the check. The [answer-engine note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/answer-engine-optimization) covers what Google does ask for, which is ordinary search work on a real page. The [GEO comparison](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/generative-engine-optimization-vs-seo) holds the research on being seen and getting the click.

## What a crawl of the files found

Ahrefs published a study in June 2026 that looked at 137,210 domains with website traffic in May 2026. (Ahrefs, 2026) About 28% of them had an llms.txt file, which came to about 38,000 valid files. Of those files, 97% got zero requests in May. Of the requests that did arrive, 96% came from bots. Named AI tools made up 19.5% of all requests, and audit or scanner tools made up 12%. We think those shares deserve a pause before you plan a project around the file. In that study most copies were never asked for. When something did ask, it was usually a bot, and only a smaller slice came from named AI tools.

We do not read this as a reason to never publish one. We read it as a reason not to expect the file to be a front door. A list that nobody asks for cannot fix a homepage that says nothing. A scanner asking for the list is not the same as a model citing you in an answer that a customer sees. The study counted requests against files, in one month, on sites that already had traffic. It is not a verdict on the idea, and it only tells us how often the file was fetched.

Publish the file if you want a clean list of your pages, but do not expect Google to read it. Keep your pages indexed and worth citing either way.

That is the order we use when we sit down with a client. Pages come first, then getting them indexed, then a sentence that a stranger can use. After that, if you still want the list, make a short file that points at those pages. Leave out drafts, tag dumps, and anything you would be ashamed to see quoted. The file is a courtesy and a way to keep control, but it is not the real work.

## A worked example

Take an independent bookshop. This is an example and not a study, so it has no score. A manager runs the floor and the website on the same tired afternoons. People ask, online and at the desk, for a book for a grieving friend. They ask for something a nine-year-old will really finish, and they ask whether tonight's reading is still on. The site has a homepage and an events page that is sometimes out of date. It also has a staff-picks page, which is the best thing they have written all year.

Someone on a forum told the manager that models will not understand the shop without llms.txt. So he made a long file. It linked every tag, every old event, and a draft page about a book club that never started. It looked thorough, but it was a bad map. A model that fetched it would have been sent to old nights and a club that does not exist. A model that never fetched it would have changed nothing, and that is the common case in the Ahrefs count. Either way, the manager would have spent his evening on the wrong thing.

If they publish a file, we would want it short. It would hold the staff-picks page. It would also hold the page that explains how to order a book the shop does not have on the shelf. It would hold the events page too, but only if the manager updates it whenever a reading is canceled. It would leave out the tag archives and the draft. The proposal, written in September 2024 and updated in August 2026, is a list of the pages you want read. The key word is "want." It does not mean everything the website software can produce.

Clear jobs keep the file honest. The owner decides which pages stand for the shop. If she would not hand a page to a regular, it stays off the list. The manager keeps the events page true, because a file that points at a lie is worse than no file. The real audience is not whoever fetches the file, or fails to fetch it. It is the person who needs a book this afternoon. So the staff-picks page has to work on its own, even if no model ever asks for the map. That is the lesson in the request counts. In the study, 97% of the valid files got zero requests in May 2026. A shop that only improved the file and left the picks page mushy would have improved the thing almost nobody asked for.

Google sits to the side of this scene on purpose. The guide says that Google does not use llms.txt for its AI features in search. So the owner could publish a lovely file and still be missing from those features. That happens if the picks page is thin, blocked, or hard to quote. The answer-engine work is the page, and the file is optional housekeeping. We would tell the manager that plainly. Then he will not buy a plugin that rebuilds the list every night from every web address it can see.

The mix of requests matters too, when someone waves a log at you. In that June 2026 study, 96% of the requests that did arrive came from bots. Named AI tools made up 19.5% of the requests, and audit or scanner tools made up 12%. A hit in a log is not a customer, since it is often a machine checking whether the file exists. Count a scanner hit as a scanner hit, and do not tell the owner it is demand.

## How we'd run it

We would first decide whether the list is worth keeping. Then we would write it by hand the first time.

First, pick the pages you hope a stranger finds, with the owner in the room. For the bookshop that means the staff picks and how to order a title the shop does not stock. It could also mean tonight's reading, but only if that page stays current. If you cannot name them without opening the website editor and scrolling, you are not ready to publish a map.

Second, make those pages good enough to quote with no file at all. They should be indexed, and they should open with clear lines. They should also have a sentence the manager would say at the desk.

## Why AI Pilots Stall After the Demo

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/why-ai-pilots-stall

Pilots stall when the data, the risk controls, or the value was never named. Surveys show use is common and scaling is rare. The demo is not the process.

An AI pilot stalls when the demo works but the daily work never does. Everyone liked what they saw in the meeting. Then Monday came, and the pilot hit real files, real handoffs, and a person who could say no.

In January 2026, Gartner wrote that at least 50% of generative AI projects were dropped after the first test run. The reasons were poor data, weak risk controls, costs that kept growing, and unclear value. (Gartner, 2026) We read that list as a plain checklist. If any of those four is blank for your pilot, it is already sliding toward the dropped pile, even if nobody has said so yet.

Our [decision guide](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check/guide/fix/ready-decision-low) fits this problem best. The steps that should come before a demo are in our [implementation framework](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-implementation-framework). The trouble we see most often is in our [data note](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/ai-ready-data). A pilot that cannot point to the one place its facts live is not early. It is unfinished, and paying for another demo will not finish it.

We have sat through the awkward meeting that follows a nice demo. The owner feels embarrassed, and the staff are tired of sample data. Someone suggests a new vendor, as if the vendor were the missing piece. The vendor was never missing. What was missing was a decision.

## Using AI is not the same as rolling it out

McKinsey's 2025 survey found that 88% of people use AI regularly in at least one part of their business. A year earlier, that number was 78%. (McKinsey) About one third of companies are rolling AI out widely. Only 23% are rolling out an AI agent system somewhere, and 39% are still trying things out. No more than 10% are rolling out agents in any single part of the business. Among companies that earn less than $100 million a year, 29% have reached the wide rollout stage. Among companies that earn more than $5 billion, it is nearly half.

Those numbers describe a stalled pilot well. Use grew fast, but only a small group of companies can run a tool every day inside one team. A small company should not hear the big-company numbers as a dare. Even the very large firms work in a different way than a dispatcher and an owner do. Your pilot may be stuck because of your own files, and that has nothing to do with how big you are.

In June 2025, Gartner said that over 40% of AI agent projects will be canceled by the end of 2027. (Gartner, 2025) We read that as a warning about projects that never became a daily habit. It does not say the software is bad. Projects get canceled when the cost, the value, or the checking stays vague after the demo. We would rather you stop a pilot on purpose this month than let it drift into that pile and blame bad luck.

Say a pilot cannot name its data, the person who checks it, and the value it brings. Then it is already in the dropped pile. Turn it into a written routine, or stop it. A third choice, like waiting to see how the next demo feels, is how the same bill keeps coming back.

## A worked example

Picture a small electrical company. This story is made up, and we did not measure it. The owner still prices the odd jobs herself. A dispatcher plans the day's routes. Two technicians send photos from the job site. An office lead turns those photos and the customers' texts into a quote whenever she can get the owner's attention.

The company paid for a pilot that turns incoming texts into a tidy intake note. In the demo, the seller pasted in three clean conversations. The note came back with the address, the problem, and a next step. Everyone nodded, and the owner pictured the office lead going home on time.

Monday looked nothing like the demo. One customer changed the light fixture in a later text. Then the same customer sent a photo of the old fixture by mistake and asked if the price included the permit. The job history lived in a group chat that the pilot could not see. The price list was a spreadsheet on the owner's laptop, named in a way only she could remember. The office lead could not tell if a summary was safe to send, because the note never said which messages it had skipped.

The data was poor in a clear way. The facts lived in many places, and the pilot acted as if they lived in one. Nobody was named to stop a quote that sounded sure but was wrong. The cost started as a small monthly fee. Then it grew when the seller offered a second task while they were already set up. The value had been described as saving the office lead's afternoon. But nobody had written down what that would look like on a Thursday when the phones were awful.

So the pilot stalled at the handoff, which is where most pilots stall. The demo had no handoff, because it ended at the summary. The real work ended when a person had to put the company's name on that summary. The office lead stopped trusting it, yet the tab stayed open. The owner kept paying, because canceling felt like admitting the demo had fooled her. It had not fooled her. It had shown her a different company, one with clean message threads and a price list the software could read.

## How we'd run it

We do not try to bring a stalled pilot back with a pep talk. We make a short decision in a set order, and we are fine if the answer is to stop.

First, we write down the original promise in one sentence. We use the words the owner remembers from the sales meeting. For the electrical company, it might be that the office lead gets an intake note she can trust from the customers' texts. If nobody can write that sentence, the pilot never had a job to do. We stop there and say so out loud, because vague hope is not worth another month of payments.

Second, we turn the four reasons projects get dropped into questions, not blame. Is the data good enough to back up the sentence? In this office, can the note see the whole message thread, the right photo, and the price list? Are the risk controls real, meaning we know who may send a quote and who must stop one? Is the cost still the cost you agreed to, or did it pick up a second task? Is the value clear enough that the office lead would notice if it went away? Any blank answer is a good reason to pause the spending.

Third, we pick the person who checks the work before we talk about a better prompt. In this office, the checker is the office lead. The owner backs her up on jobs above the dollar line they already use for quotes done by hand. If nobody can name that person, the pilot is only a toy. We also sit with her and watch her handle one real message thread. Watching can bruise the seller's story, but it is very kind to the business.

Fourth, we choose a written routine or a stop, and we do it in the same meeting. A written routine says which places the note may pull from. It names the message thread, the photo rule, and the price list, and the office lead still sends every quote. A stop means the subscription ends.

… Full post: https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/why-ai-pilots-stall

Sources
1. Why generative AI projects fail after proof of concept — Gartner, 2026-01-26 — https://www.gartner.com/en/articles/genai-project-failure
2. The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation — McKinsey — https://www.mckinsey.com/~/media/mckinsey/business%20functions/quantumblack/our%20insights/the%20state%20of%20ai/november%202025/the-state-of-ai-2025-agents-innovation_cmyk-v1.pdf
3. Over 40 percent of agentic AI projects will be canceled by end of 2027 — Gartner, 2025-06-25 — https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-25-gartner-predicts-over-40-percent-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-canceled-by-end-of-2027

## Why We Build on Cloudflare: Security, AI and the Edge

https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/why-we-build-on-cloudflare

Our site, our Readiness Check and HQ all run on Cloudflare. Here is what the platform gives us for safety, AI tools, data and cost, with sources.

Here is the short answer. We build on Cloudflare® because one platform gives us the safety, the AI tools, the data and the global network our work needs. Our own site, our Readiness Check and HQ, the app we use to run client work, all run on it. That lets us spend our time on the job in front of us, not on servers.

This note walks through the three reasons. First comes the safety you get by default. Next are the AI tools, and last is the platform itself, with what it costs. Each claim links to a Cloudflare page, and we say plainly which tools we use today and which we only plan to use. If you want to know whether your business is ready to put AI to work, the [Readiness Check](https://check.abra-ca-dabra.app/check) takes five to seven minutes.

## What do we actually run on Cloudflare?

Every app we run lives on Cloudflare Workers®, which is code that runs on the Cloudflare network instead of on one server. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) Our marketing site is a Worker that serves its pages and talks to a second Worker for the chat. The chat uses Workers AI® for speech to text, Durable Objects™ to hold each chat, and Turnstile to keep bots out.

The Readiness Check is its own Worker. It keeps results in a D1 database and hands longer reads of a website to a queue, so a big job does not hold up the page. HQ is a Worker too. It uses D1 for its records, R2 to store files, and Workers AI and AI Gateway for its AI calls. The agents behind HQ are built on the Cloudflare Agents SDK. If you want the full story of how work moves through HQ, read [how client work moves through HQ and our AI agents](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/how-client-work-flows-through-hq).

## What safety comes built in?

Most of it is on before we write a line of code. Cloudflare finds and stops DDoS attacks on its own, and its docs say this is on for all plans. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) A DDoS attack is a flood of fake traffic meant to knock a site over. When the site sits behind Cloudflare, that flood hits the Cloudflare network first.

The WAF, or web app firewall, checks each request against sets of rules and filters out the bad ones. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) You can turn on managed rules that Cloudflare keeps up to date, and add your own rules and rate limits. Bot tools sort real people from scripts that scrape content or try stolen passwords. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) Free plans get a simple bot switch, and Enterprise plans get a score for each request.

TLS is the lock in your browser bar. Cloudflare issues free certificates through Universal SSL, so traffic between visitors and the site is encrypted. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) For our chat we use Turnstile, which checks that a visitor is a person without making them solve a puzzle. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) The chat asks for a Turnstile pass when it opens, and a fresh one before each voice call.

For tools only our team should reach, there is Zero Trust. Cloudflare One checks who you are before it lets each request in, instead of trusting anyone who is already inside the network. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) Its Access tool guards the private tool server that HQ connects to, and HQ shows a service token to get in.

## Which AI tools does Cloudflare offer?

Cloudflare now has a full set of AI tools that run on the same network as the app. Workers AI runs open models on Cloudflare's GPUs, and you pay for what you use. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) We use it in HQ and in our chat. AI Gateway sits between an app and the models it calls. It logs each call, shows cost, caches answers, limits rates, and can retry or fall back to a second model when one fails. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) HQ sends its AI calls through it.

The Agents SDK is how we build agents. Cloudflare says each agent gets its own lasting identity, its own SQL storage, live connections and scheduled work. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) That is a good fit for agents that keep working on a task over days, which is what ours do.

There are more tools we reach for when a job needs them. We do not use these in our own stack today. Vectorize is a vector database, which stores what text or images mean so an app can find close matches. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) AI Search, which used to be called AutoRAG, was renamed in Cloudflare's changelog. (Cloudflare Changelog, 2025) It lets an app or an agent search its own files in plain words, with keyword and meaning search turned on together. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) Browser Run, which used to be called Browser Rendering, runs real browsers on the network so code or agents can read pages, take screenshots and fill in forms. (Cloudflare Blog, 2026) (Cloudflare Docs, 2026)

AI Crawl Control works the other way round. It shows which AI services are reading your site, lets you allow or block each crawler, and tracks which ones follow your robots.txt file. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) That matters for AI search, and it ties into the work we do on [AI visibility](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/services/ai-visibility/) and files like [llms.txt](https://abra-ca-dabra.app/blog/what-is-llms-txt).

## Why Workers, D1, R2 and Durable Objects?

Each one does a plain job, and they all plug into a Worker with a few lines of setup. D1 is a SQL database that the docs say you can roll back to any minute in the last 30 days. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) R2 stores files and does not charge to send them out to the web. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) Durable Objects pair a bit of code with its own storage, so a chat or an agent keeps its state in one place. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) Queues let one Worker hand a job to another and make sure it gets done. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026)

This is how the Readiness Check handles longer reads of a website, so they do not make you wait. The page hands the job to a queue, and Workers pick it up in small parts. The results land in D1, and the page reads them back as they come in.

## How fast is the network?

Cloudflare says that 95% of people online are within 50 milliseconds of one of its data centers. (Cloudflare) That is Cloudflare's own figure, not one we measured. What we can say is how it shapes our work. Our code runs close to the visitor by default, so we do not pick a region or move servers when a client grows.

## What does it cost?

It starts small. The Workers paid plan has a minimum charge of $5 a month per account, with usage above that billed as you go. (Cloudflare Docs, 2026) The same page says requests for static files, like images and pages, are free, and there is no charge for data sent out. The free plan also includes some use each day. Prices change, so check the pricing page before you plan a budget.

For our clients, the point is that cost tracks use. A new tool does not need a big server bill on day one. It can start small and grow, and the bill grows with it.

## Should your business build on Cloudflare?

If you need a custom app, an AI assistant, or an agent that does real work, it is a strong place to start.
